title: Medical Biochemical Genetics Fellowship

prerequisites.learnerLevel: Advanced graduate medical education / post-residency clinician self-study, designed as an independent edX-style course. Not an entry-level clinical course.
recommendedPriorKnowledge: MD/DO or equivalent clinical medicine background for physician-track context (not a credential prerequisite to browse the independent educational course).
Completed core medical genetics/genomics residency level; prior biochemistry, molecular genetics, clinical laboratory interpretation and pediatric/adult medicine are assumed.
Basic acid-base, nutrition/catabolism, inheritance, pedigree and molecular diagnostic methods.
prerequisites.formalFellowshipEligibility: This course does not establish formal fellowship or ABMGG examination eligibility. The board requires qualifying accredited training.

objectives: Construct a differential for suspected inherited metabolic disease across neonatal, pediatric and adult presentations using history, pedigree and biochemical patterns.
Choose and interpret screening, biochemical, enzymatic, molecular and functional tests with attention to specimen, pre-analytic, method and age-related limitations.
Integrate all 15 current ABMGG blueprint domains into a structured study plan and recognize overlaps.
Explain why screening results are not definitive diagnosis and use current official ACT sheets/local screening follow-up pathways.
Synthesize a family-centered, evidence-aware educational plan while recognizing clinical, professional and scope boundaries.
Differentiate physician Medical Biochemical Genetics subspecialty from laboratory Clinical Biochemical Genetics, and describe documented training/board qualifications without overclaiming.

units.title: Biochemical genetics clinical reasoning and acute metabolic presentations
objectives: Construct a life-stage-aware differential from catabolic trigger, fasting tolerance, neurologic/hepatic/cardiac features, and family history.
Distinguish pattern recognition from diagnosis; use first-line screening tests and urgent consultation safely.
topics: Phenotype-to-pathway reasoning; age-of-onset; catabolism; glucose, blood gas, electrolytes/anion gap, lactate, ammonia, ketones, liver tests, plasma amino acids, acylcarnitines, urine organic acids.
boardDomains: All domains; ACGME Patient Care/Medical Knowledge
casePractice: Fictional acute decompensation vignette; build prioritized differential and next-test table.
units.assessment: Timed case synthesis: justify the top three pathways, name discriminating tests and limitations, identify urgent escalation, and avoid a single-test diagnosis.

units.title: Amino acids I: phenylalanine, tyrosine, branched-chain amino acids and glycine
objectives: Interpret elevated phenylalanine with follow-up testing for PAH deficiency versus BH4 synthesis/recycling disorders.
Relate branched-chain amino acid catabolism and glycine metabolism to clinical/laboratory patterns.
topics: PAH/PKU and treatment monitoring principles; BH4/cofactor differential; tyrosinemias; MSUD; glycine encephalopathy; newborn screening ACT-sheet reasoning.
casePractice: ACMG screen-positive phenylalanine and leucine ACT-sheet cases; no copied patient data.
units.assessment: One-page biochemical differential for Phe or leucine flags: pattern, confirmatory strategy, inheritance, and major caveat.

units.title: Amino acids II: urea cycle, homocysteine, transport and serine
objectives: Differentiate hyperammonemia due to urea-cycle disorders from organic acidemia and other causes using acid-base/ketone and amino-acid patterns.
Interpret citrulline, arginine, ornithine, urine orotic acid and methionine/homocysteine as components of a differential, not standalone proof.
topics: Urea cycle enzymes/transporters; OTC versus proximal/distal patterns; citrullinemia; argininosuccinic aciduria; argininemia; homocystinuria/remethylation; amino-acid transport; serine.
casePractice: Fictional ammonia case; contrast high/low citrulline patterns and identify confirmatory testing.
units.assessment: Interpret a fictional metabolite panel and state what it can and cannot distinguish.

units.title: Organic acids, ketone metabolism and emergency patterns
objectives: Distinguish organic acidemias from urea-cycle defects and fatty-acid oxidation defects using acid-base, ketones, ammonia, acylcarnitines and organic acids.
Explain broad classes of organic-acid and ketone-body disorders and laboratory confirmation.
topics: MMA/propionic acidemia, cobalamin defects, IVA/C5, 3-MCC/C5OH, glutaric acidemia I, HMG-CoA lyase/SCOT, other organic acids; acute versus stable-state samples.
casePractice: ACMG C3, C5, C5OH or related public ACT sheets; link is to official current index.
units.assessment: Pattern-match exercise with safeguards against overinterpreting one acylcarnitine or urine peak.

units.title: Fatty-acid oxidation, carnitine transport and lipid metabolism
objectives: Recognize fasting/illness-associated hypoketotic hypoglycemia as a pathway clue while retaining non-IEM differentials.
Map acylcarnitine patterns to chain-length classes, carnitine transport and confirmatory biochemical/molecular methods.
topics: MCAD, VLCAD, LCHAD/TFP, CPT I/II, CACT, primary carnitine deficiency, multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; hyperlipidemias; cholesterol/bile-acid pathways.
casePractice: Fictional acylcarnitine profile plus fasting event; contrast FAO defect and ketogenesis disorders.
units.assessment: Structured report: candidate pathways, confirmatory strategy, status/age/catabolic confounders, and counseling/referral questions.

units.title: Carbohydrates, glycogen, glycolysis and glycosylation
objectives: Use fasting/postprandial context and organ involvement to discriminate carbohydrate disorders.
Explain selected glycogenoses, glycolytic/gluconeogenic disorders, galactose/fructose disease and congenital glycosylation disorders.
topics: GSD except Pompe (LSD unit); glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, galactose/fructose, pentose phosphate, CDG; biochemical versus genetic confirmation.
casePractice: Fictional hepatomegaly/hypoglycemia or infant feeding scenario; propose discriminator.
units.assessment: Compare two pathways in a matrix; address testing context and limits.

units.title: Cofactors: cobalamin, biotin, biopterin, molybdenum and vitamins
objectives: Explain cofactor roles in selected metabolic pathways and predict multi-metabolite patterns when cofactor availability/recycling fails.
Distinguish selected intracellular cobalamin and B-vitamin responsive disorders from enzyme defects without assuming a treatment response proves diagnosis.
topics: Cobalamin synthesis/processing and MMA/homocysteine; biotin/holocarboxylase; BH4; molybdenum cofactor/sulfite; folate, pyridoxine, riboflavin, niacin, thiamine; safe evidence-based confirmation.
casePractice: Official ACMG methionine/citrulline/Phe ACT sheets; compare convergent pathways.
units.assessment: Pathway map plus differential table. The course does not prescribe empiric dosing or replace acute-care protocols.

units.title: Lysosomal storage, peroxisomal and lipid-storage disease
objectives: Relate substrate accumulation, enzyme function, trafficking, and organ-level phenotype in lysosomal diseases.
Differentiate lysosomal disorders, peroxisomal biogenesis/single-enzyme disease, and related mimics using fit-for-purpose assays and sequencing.
topics: MPS, sphingolipidoses, multiple enzyme deficiencies, Pompe/cystinosis/NCL; Zellweger spectrum, X-ALD, Refsum; enzyme, substrate, biomarker and molecular test roles.
casePractice: MedPix/Open-i case reports and image records; use only learner-side, lawful viewing and case-specific license check.
units.assessment: Create diagnostic test strategy for a fictional multisystem phenotype; cite source and not infer diagnosis from an image alone.

units.title: Mitochondrial energy metabolism and mitochondrial disease
objectives: Interpret lactate/pyruvate and bioenergetic data in physiologic and pre-analytic context.
Compare mtDNA, nuclear genes, heteroplasmy, mtDNA maintenance/depletion, and respiratory-chain assembly categories.
topics: Mitochondrial myopathy, Leigh, adult presentations, OXPHOS/assembly, mtDNA variants and maintenance/depletion, MELAS; lab methods and tissue considerations.
casePractice: Fictional multisystem phenotype with nonspecific elevated lactate; design differential and avoid overcalling.
units.assessment: Short interpretive memo including pre-analytic limitations and two alternative explanations.

units.title: Purines, pyrimidines, creatine, neurotransmitters and metals
objectives: Relate pathway intermediates to purine/pyrimidine, creatine, neurotransmitter and metal homeostasis disorders.
Select appropriate fluid, metabolite or molecular test and articulate age/medication/collection constraints.
topics: Lesch-Nyhan, ADA, UMP synthase; creatine biosynthesis/transport; neurotransmitter and GABA metabolism; copper (Wilson/Menkes), iron, zinc; diagnostic pitfalls.
boardDomains: IX Purines/pyrimidines (3%); XI Creatine (1%); XII Neurotransmitters (2%); XIII Metals (3%)
casePractice: A public case report or anonymized educational record selected via MedPix/Open-i; rights checked before display.
units.assessment: Select a confirmatory approach and interpret ambiguity; separate gene-level evidence from biochemical phenotype.

units.title: Biochemical genetics laboratory methods, quality and result interpretation
objectives: Compare screening, targeted biochemical, enzyme, molecular and functional tests; evaluate sensitivity, specificity, specimen timing and differential.
Identify pre-analytic/analytic artifacts and communicate a safe, clear interpretive report.
topics: MS/MS and acylcarnitines; amino-acid chromatography; urine organic acids/GC-MS; enzyme assays; NGS/variant interpretation; QA/QC, artifacts, method limits, regulation and lab-clinician collaboration.
boardDomains: XIV Laboratory (8%); ACGME laboratory instruction and advanced interpretation
casePractice: Fictional de-identified lab tables only; no patient record or clinical result copied.
units.assessment: Laboratory interpretation exercise graded for evidence, pre-analytics, test limitation and communication.

units.title: Lifespan management, counseling, ethics, systems and scholarship
objectives: Synthesize family history/pedigree, reproductive and psychosocial context, transition-to-adult care, multidisciplinary roles, evidence appraisal and follow-up.
Explain the boundary between educational case planning and clinician-directed, individualized care.
topics: Inpatient/outpatient pathway; longitudinal and adult disease; family-centered communication; informed consent; uncertainty; newborn-screen systems; multidisciplinary coordination; research literacy and ACGME professionalism.
Other biochemical-genetics disease category in the current blueprint; consult the effective exam-year blueprint for inclusions.
boardDomains: Across all domains; ACGME Professionalism, Systems-Based Practice, Practice-Based Learning
casePractice: Role-play counseling with fictional family; no real family data.
units.assessment: Capstone oral defense: differential, testing, uncertainty, family communication, and care-team escalation.

assignment.title: Integrated metabolic-genetics case portfolio (fictional, educational scenarios only)
deliverables: Three written differential-and-test plans: hyperammonemia, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, and positive amino-acid screen.
One laboratory interpretation memo citing assay limitations and at least two competing explanations.
One family communication script that explains uncertainty and referral/follow-up without treatment orders.
One 10-minute capstone oral presentation with a board-domain map and source citations.

rubric.excellent: Mechanism explains findings; key competing pathways and red flags included; uncertainty explicit.
Tests are linked to a question; specimen/pre-analytic and analytic limitations included; screening distinguished from confirmation.
No premature diagnosis; appropriate urgency/escalation, multidisciplinary/local-protocol caveat and lifespan perspective.
Plain-language, non-alarmist, culturally responsive explanation; no copied patient data or advice beyond scope.
Current primary authoritative sources cited; correct blueprint domain mapping; exact board terms preserved.

assignment.scoring: Rubric assesses educational reasoning only. It is not an entrustment, competency, board-readiness, licensure or clinical performance instrument.

components.name: Unit retrieval quizzes
components.format: Short answer and multiple choice; feedback cites source.

components.name: Case/laboratory portfolio
components.format: Fictional patterns; graded using assignment rubric.

components.name: Original practice set
components.format: 10 questions, rationales; formative and not validated.

components.name: Capstone synthesis
components.format: Oral written submission across patient care, interpretation, limits, board map and evidence.

assessment.suggestedCourseCompletionThreshold: 80% of available educational points is a self-study target only; not a board-passing predictor, validated exam score, clinical competence determination or guarantee.

studyHours.breakdown: Suggested 120 hours total self-study plan: 18.51 verified free recorded-video hours; 44.99 hours reading; 30 hours unit notes/problem solving; 18 hours portfolio/capstone; 8.5 hours review. This is an independent learning plan, not an official JH curriculum or clinical training duration.

mapping.name: Medical Biochemical Genetics Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Exact fellowship URL retained from the MED-085 item packet. The current official JH program page was independently read at https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/genetic-medicine/education-training/clinical-genetics-residency-program/residency-program/medical-biochemical-genetics-fellowship. It states a one-year ACGME-accredited physician fellowship, available after medical genetics residency, with inpatient/outpatient clinical training, Maryland State Newborn Screening Laboratory and Kennedy Krieger Institute Biochemical Genetics Laboratory experience, independent research time, and ABMGG Medical Biochemical Genetics exam qualification after fellowship completion. Public page is a program summary, not a full curricular schedule or independently verified current ADS record.

topicGaps: 36-hour floor remains unmet: verified free public full-length recordings with exact observed duration total 18.510444 h (18.510444 h foundation, 0.000000 h specialty, 0.000000 h supplementary); residual 17.489556 h. No screened candidate was added to the counted media ledger because ordinary public access/duration evidence was incomplete. The SIMD 2026 MBG archive is unusually well-matched and supplies direct watch links and transcripts for some videos, but its player/runtime could not be verified here without bypassing YouTube restrictions; exact durations must not be inferred from last transcript cue.

Domain-level instruction remains incomplete: the original 12-unit syllabus maps the blueprint, but lacks a full specialist course depth across all conditions. Top priorities for recording/qualified review are cofactor and organic-acid differential interpretation; lysosomal/peroxisomal assay pitfalls; mitochondrial tissue/pre-analytic interpretation; noncanonical transport, creatine, neurotransmitter and metals; and adult presentations/longitudinal systems. Blueprint XV ‘Other disease category’ is intentionally unspecified.

The 2026 SIMD/Children's Colorado MBG core seminar is publicized as a 21-session series. The CE page says sessions are archived for asynchronous learning; direct course content shows numerous items locked and at $25/session (with different prices in the listing), requiring registration. A $0 series headline does not establish free anonymous video access; the recordings were not counted. Check access and per-session terms directly; no login was used.

Newborn-screening RUSP information on HRSA's cited page is archival after the committee ended in March 2025; state panel and follow-up pathways vary. Use current state program instructions and current ACMG ACT sheets.
Human clinician review has not been performed. The authored episodes are educational scripts, not protocols, treatment instructions, validation of clinical decisions, or examination items.

boardNames: American Board of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ABMGG) — Medical Biochemical Genetics subspecialty certification examination (ABMGG labels the linked exam Clinical/Medical Biochemical Genetics).
medical.boardStatus: Distinct ABMGG physician subspecialty certification exam exists. ABMGG’s official 2026 Dates & Fees page states Clinical/Medical Biochemical Genetics is offered during the 2027 examination cycle. The 2025 ABMGG biochemical genetics blueprint is the source for the 2026 examination-cycle content. As of 2026-10-07, the exact board exam label in the current board schedule is “Clinical/Medical Biochemical Genetics”; ABMGG pathway/specialty pages identify Medical Biochemical Genetics as the physician subspecialty and Clinical Biochemical Genetics as a separate laboratory specialty.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABMGG says Medical Biochemical Genetics requires one year of accredited subspecialty training and is available only to physicians who completed a clinical genetics and genomics residency; this course confers no eligibility. Confirm current individual credentials and policy with ABMGG. Clinical Biochemical Genetics is a distinct laboratory specialty, not a synonym for this physician fellowship.

officialProgrammes.name: Medical Biochemical Genetics Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Exact fellowship URL retained from the MED-085 item packet. The current official JH program page was independently read at https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/genetic-medicine/education-training/clinical-genetics-residency-program/residency-program/medical-biochemical-genetics-fellowship. It states a one-year ACGME-accredited physician fellowship, available after medical genetics residency, with inpatient/outpatient clinical training, Maryland State Newborn Screening Laboratory and Kennedy Krieger Institute Biochemical Genetics Laboratory experience, independent research time, and ABMGG Medical Biochemical Genetics exam qualification after fellowship completion. Public page is a program summary, not a full curricular schedule or independently verified current ADS record.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One exact Johns Hopkins clinical physician fellowship from the supplied packet. No Harvard variant, Clinical Biochemical Genetics laboratory fellowship, research-only postdoctoral position, non-physician track, or generic directory label is conflated with this physician fellowship. Exact packet URL preserved; current official JH page is linked in notes. Directory accreditation label not treated as individual verification.
sourceCaveats: ACGME Medical Biochemical Genetics program requirements are a national accreditation standard, not evidence that every item is the detailed Johns Hopkins public curriculum. JH publicly gives a program summary; we did not verify current ADS listing or hidden schedules.

The ABMGG board pathway/examination and ACGME accreditation are not interchangeable. ABMGG 2025 biochemical blueprint effective August 2025 is used; official cycle page reports 2027 offering for the combined Clinical/Medical Biochemical Genetics exam. Verify changes at ABMGG before applying.
ABMGG separates physician Medical Biochemical Genetics from laboratory Clinical Biochemical Genetics. No laboratory fellowship or research-only role counted as this physician specialty.
HRSA RUSP page is explicitly archival (committee terminated March 2025); state panels and follow-up vary. Check current state newborn-screening instructions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn-screening report flags elevated phenylalanine. Which statement is the most defensible next-step principle?

options.text: The screen alone establishes PAH deficiency.
Treat the screening flag as a signal; follow the current ACT/local pathway and distinguish PAH from BH4 synthesis or recycling disorders.
A normal physical examination excludes a metabolic disorder.
A single repeat screen replaces confirmatory evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABMGG blueprint includes PKU/hyperphenylalaninemia and BH4 synthesis/regeneration; a screen-positive result requires appropriate confirmatory evaluation rather than diagnostic labeling. [1] [2]

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional infant has marked hyperammonemia. Which additional pattern most supports a urea-cycle disorder over a typical organic acidemia, while not proving it?

options.text: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis with prominent ketosis
Respiratory alkalosis or relatively preserved acid-base status, low citrulline pattern in some proximal defects, and no characteristic organic-acid pattern
A positive urine ketone alone
Isolated elevated lactate proves a urea-cycle defect

practiceQuestions.rationale: Typical differentiating patterns include acid-base state, ketones, amino acids and urine organic acids; overlap exists, so no single pattern is definitive. [3] [4]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which set is most useful as a first-line pattern-oriented assessment when an IEM is suspected in an acutely ill patient?

options.text: Glucose, electrolytes/anion gap, blood gas as indicated, ammonia, lactate, ketones, liver tests, plasma amino acids, urine organic acids and acylcarnitines as context dictates
Only a broad genetic panel
Only urine pH
A fasting challenge performed without specialist supervision

practiceQuestions.rationale: The free MSD professional diagnostic overview describes basic tests, followed by specific biochemical and confirmatory testing; risky challenge tests belong only in controlled settings. [5]

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypoketotic hypoglycemia pattern during illness should primarily prompt consideration of which broad pathway class?

options.text: Fatty-acid oxidation/ketogenesis disorders among other differential diagnoses
A lysosomal storage disorder as the only possible cause
A diagnosis of MCAD deficiency without testing
A specific gene variant inferred from symptoms alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fasting-related hypoketotic hypoglycemia is a pathway clue, not a specific diagnosis; use acylcarnitines, clinical context and confirmatory studies. [1] [6]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about a positive newborn screen is correct?

options.text: Every state screens an identical panel and follows a uniform treatment protocol.
The RUSP is a federally recommended panel; states ultimately determine their screening panels, and follow-up is program-specific.
The RUSP itself certifies subspecialists.
A screen-positive test always means disease is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: HRSA explains the recommended RUSP and state authority to determine screening panels; screening is not diagnosis. The RUSP page is archival and flagged as no longer active, so link is used for the scope statement, not current policy changes. [7]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which assay strategy can provide a mechanistic complement when an enzyme deficiency is suspected in an LSD?

options.text: Appropriate enzyme activity and substrate/biomarker studies, interpreted with phenotype and molecular testing as needed
CBC alone
MRI alone
A pathogenic variant in any gene associated with storage disease regardless of phenotype

practiceQuestions.rationale: Diagnosis commonly integrates phenotype, specific biochemical/enzyme testing and molecular data; a test must fit the hypothesis. [1] [8]

practiceQuestions.stem: An elevated lactate is found in a patient with exercise intolerance. Which approach is best?

options.text: Diagnose mitochondrial disease from one lactate measurement.
Consider collection/pre-analytic context, physiologic state and alternatives; interpret lactate/pyruvate and broader biochemical/molecular data with specialist input.
Ignore the finding because lactate is never useful.
Assume any high lactate proves mtDNA disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lactate is nonspecific; context and pre-analytics matter, and mitochondrial disease has genetic and biochemical heterogeneity. [1] [9]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description correctly distinguishes the physician Medical Biochemical Genetics fellowship from Clinical Biochemical Genetics?

options.text: They are identical program names for one laboratory specialty.
Medical Biochemical Genetics is a physician subspecialty after clinical genetics residency; Clinical Biochemical Genetics is an ABMGG laboratory specialty with separate training pathway.
Both are generic directory categories without certification.
Medical Biochemical Genetics is a research-only postdoc.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABMGG calls Medical Biochemical Genetics a physician subspecialty and Clinical Biochemical Genetics a separate laboratory specialty; the Johns Hopkins page describes a one-year physician fellowship. [10] [11] [12]

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees an Open-i image in a paper and wishes to place it in a new course handout. What is the correct rights approach?

options.text: Open-i makes every image public domain.
Check the individual image/article license; Open-i itself does not grant permission. Link to the original or obtain permission where required.
Remove the citation and crop the image.
Assume de-identification permits unrestricted republication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Open-i FAQ states copyright remains with authors/journals and reuse depends on the particular license; free-to-view is not rehosting permission. [13]

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the board exam is accurate as of the course date check (2026-10-07)?

options.text: No separate examination exists for Medical Biochemical Genetics.

ABMGG offers a dedicated Medical/Clinical Biochemical Genetics subspecialty/specialty exam; its official schedule says the next combined Clinical/Medical Biochemical Genetics offering is in the 2027 cycle.
The ACGME issues the board certification.
Completing this independent course creates ABMGG eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABMGG maintains the biochemical genetics exam blueprint and official dates page; pathway eligibility requires accredited training. This course confers no eligibility. [1] [10] [12]

title: Nephrology Fellowship Program
level: Adult clinical physician subspecialty fellowship self-study; based on Johns Hopkins general nephrology fellowship, not institutional training-aligned independent study

prerequisites.audience: Advanced medical learners and postgraduate physicians studying adult nephrology; primary intended level is post-internal-medicine resident/fellow. Not a substitute for training.
requiredKnowledge: Internal medicine, cardiovascular and endocrine physiology
Renal anatomy, basic electrolyte/acid-base interpretation and evidence appraisal
Comfort with SI and conventional units; basic epidemiology
prerequisites.accessibility: Independent self-study; public official curricula/guidelines linked; no patient access, procedures, rotations, supervision, credentialing or confidential Hopkins course materials.

objectives: Interpret kidney function, albuminuria, urinalysis and urine sediment in time and clinical context.
Reason through sodium/water, acid-base, potassium, mineral, hypertension and stone problems using differential diagnoses.
Classify AKI and CKD and appraise glomerular, tubulointerstitial, cystic, transplant and dialysis topics aligned to ABIM’s published blueprint.
Use current guideline versions and distinguish final guidance from drafts or superseded chapters.
Communicate diagnostic uncertainty, equity, ethics and patient-centered modality choices.
Distinguish institutional fellowship tracks, ACGME requirements and ABIM certification from this course.

units.title: Renal physiology, filtration and measurement
objectives: Relate nephron segment function, glomerular hemodynamics and autoregulation to observed filtration and tubular handling.
Compare creatinine-based estimates, cystatin C context, albuminuria/proteinuria and measured clearance; state limitations.
topics: GFR, renal blood flow, autoregulation, filtration fraction, tubular transport; kidney-function biomarkers and assay/clinical confounders.
units.casePractice: Fictional trend table: explain why one creatinine value cannot establish chronicity or etiology.
units.assessment: Concept map scored for physiology, measure choice, caveat and citations (0–4 each; ≥3 each).

units.title: Diagnostic approach, urinalysis and urine sediment
objectives: Construct a problem representation from history, medication exposure, hemodynamics, urine, serum, imaging and time course.
Interpret sediment patterns probabilistically and identify when biopsy/imaging or urgent escalation may be considered by clinicians.
topics: Hematuria/proteinuria, casts, dysmorphic cells, urine indices, imaging/obstruction, biopsy indication/risk, diagnostic uncertainty.
units.casePractice: Source-linked external urine sediment atlas and Radiopaedia linked examples; no copied images.
units.assessment: Differential worksheet: pattern, alternatives, next discriminating evidence, safety/uncertainty (4 domains).

units.title: Sodium, water and volume disorders
objectives: Classify dysnatremia by tonicity and volume context, distinguishing water diuresis from osmotic diuresis.
Use a structured approach to hyponatremia/hypernatremia and edema/salt depletion without prescribing patient-specific correction.
topics: Hyponatremia, hypernatremia, osmolality, SIAD, water diuresis, salt excess/depletion, edema, polyuria.
boardDomains: ABIM Sodium and Water Abnormalities (8%); CKD
units.casePractice: Fictional sodium/osmolality worksheet with units and missing data explicitly marked.
units.assessment: Algorithm rubric: tonicity, volume category, mechanism, risk/uncertainty, dated source.

units.title: Acid–base, potassium, calcium/phosphate/magnesium and stones
objectives: Classify acid-base disorders and recognize mixed processes using a transparent calculation sequence.
Differentiate renal from nonrenal potassium and mineral disturbances and map stone risk to metabolic evaluation.
topics: Anion gap, compensation, RTA, hyper/hypokalemia, calcium/phosphate/magnesium, CKD-MBD, nephrolithiasis.
boardDomains: ABIM Acid-Base and Potassium (9%); Calcium/Phosphorus/Magnesium and Stones (4%)
units.casePractice: Fictional lab cases for AG/corrected calculations; use reference intervals on each case.
units.assessment: Calculation sheet scored for calculations, explanation, differential, no unsupported management order.

units.title: AKI, critical care nephrology and kidney replacement therapy
objectives: Differentiate hemodynamic, parenchymal and postrenal AKI using time course and evidence, with multifactorial diagnoses retained.
Explain RRT modalities, indications, prescription variables and complications at a conceptual level.
topics: AKI/AKD continuum; prerenal/intrinsic/postrenal; urine microscopy; nephrotoxins; ICU fluids/hemodynamics; intermittent HD/CRRT; timing and stopping RRT.
units.casePractice: Fictional ICU data table; do not use real patient orders.
units.assessment: Case conference memo scored for etiologic reasoning, alternatives, RRT indication concepts, escalation and source currency.

units.title: CKD detection, staging, progression and risk
objectives: Apply KDIGO 2024 CGA concepts and chronicity evidence; interpret eGFR and albuminuria categories together.
Explain progression-risk assessment, uncertainty, referral context and the guideline update caveat.
topics: CKD definition/chronicity, cause-GFR-albuminuria (CGA), eGFR limitations, risk prediction, AKI-CKD, care equity.
units.casePractice: Fictional longitudinal eGFR/uACR table; compare category-based and risk-based interpretation.
units.assessment: Risk communication one-pager with chronicity, categories, caveat, source date and equity consideration.

units.title: Chronic kidney failure, dialysis and conservative kidney care
objectives: Compare hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, home modalities, transplant and conservative kidney management as care pathways.
Explain access, adequacy, complications and shared decision-making without claiming hands-on procedural competence.
topics: ESKD planning, dialysis initiation/discontinuation, HD/PD prescription principles, vascular access, water, peritonitis, home HD, conservative care, ethics.
units.casePractice: Fictional modality-preference decision aid; no patient identifiers.
units.assessment: Comparison matrix rubric: modality mechanics, risks, patient priorities, equity, careful non-prescriptive wording.

units.title: Hypertension and renal vascular disease
objectives: Build a differential for common and secondary hypertension in kidney disease.
Interpret renovascular and end-organ clues and summarize guideline differences without equating association with causation.
topics: Essential/resistant/secondary HTN, renovascular causes, endocrine/genetic causes, pregnancy, CKD-related HTN.
units.casePractice: Fictional BP/medication timeline with measurement-context limitations.
units.assessment: Differential board: common/urgent alternatives, test rationale, contraindications and source date.

units.title: Glomerular disease, vasculitis and thrombotic microangiopathy
objectives: Organize nephritic and nephrotic syndromes, serology and biopsy findings into differential diagnoses.
Compare current KDIGO chapter updates (IgAN/IgAV 2025, LN/ANCA 2024) and distinguish evidence/approval changes.
topics: IgAN/IgAV, lupus, ANCA, anti-GBM, infection-related GN, membranous, FSGS, MCD, paraprotein disease, complement/TMA, biopsy interpretation.
units.casePractice: Radiopaedia rID 47562 transplant case linked for differential exercise; pathology educational material source-link only.
units.assessment: Evidence matrix: syndrome, tests, biopsy role, current guideline version, uncertainty.

units.title: Tubular, interstitial, cystic and inherited disease
objectives: Recognize tubulopathies, drug-induced interstitial injury, obstruction and inherited cystic phenotypes.
Describe relevant clinical, imaging, genetic and family-history limitations.
topics: RTA/Fanconi, acute/chronic interstitial nephritis, toxins, ADPKD, renal masses/cysts, nephrolithiasis.
units.casePractice: Optional linked renal imaging cases and TCIA KIRC images (dataset-specific CC BY 3.0; do not download/rehost into course).
units.assessment: One-page syndrome map separating imaging observation, likely cause and confirmatory evidence.

units.title: Kidney transplantation and allograft dysfunction
objectives: Describe candidate/donor assessment and transplant immunology at a board-concept level.
Structure differential of allograft dysfunction, balancing rejection, infection, drug toxicity, recurrent disease and obstruction.
topics: Alloimmunity, allocation, living donor risk, induction/maintenance immunosuppression, rejection types, graft dysfunction, infection, pregnancy/fertility.
units.casePractice: Radiopaedia rID 47562 authentic case link; image reuse conditions apply.
units.assessment: Differential matrix scored for competing diagnoses, timing/context, test limits, immunosuppression risks, citations.

units.title: Nephropharmacology, communication, quality and evidence literacy
objectives: Explain renal drug clearance/dialytic removal and common nephrotoxic mechanisms; reconcile guideline/label dates.
Communicate uncertainty, patient values, health inequities and evidence limitations; produce a quality-improvement question.
topics: Drug dosing concepts, nephrotoxins, dialysis removal, guideline appraisal, care transitions, ethics, equity, QI, research design.
units.casePractice: Text-only constructed scenarios; no patient records or unauthorized images.
units.assessment: Capstone: evidence-to-decision brief and short oral handoff; rubric below.

assignment.title: Nephrology evidence-to-reasoning portfolio
deliverables: Four short problem representations: fictional AKI, dysnatremia, glomerular syndrome and allograft dysfunction.
One CKD CGA/risk interpretation worksheet with explicit dates, units, and guideline version.
One dialysis modality comparison designed around fictional patient preferences, without individual treatment directives.
One evidence table that reconciles KDIGO updates and the ABIM blueprint; cite all claims.
A 5-minute recorded or written teaching explanation using only original diagrams/text; no external patient images copied.
assignment.passThreshold: 80/100 and no critical safety/provenance error; educational benchmark only, not validated or board-predictive.

assessment.formative: Ten original single-best-answer items with explanations (see practiceQuestions); self-checks per unit and retrieval practice; no pass prediction.
assessment.summative: Portfolio + 10-question original quiz; target 80% for course completion only.
assessment.rubric: Accuracy, mechanism-based reasoning, alternatives, guideline currency, uncertainty, equity, ethics and clear communication.
assessment.validityLimit: Neither assessment is an official ABIM examination or validated predictor; no patient-care competence or credential is conferred.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exactly the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine general Nephrology Fellowship Program. Its four tracks (Clinical/Epidemiological Investigation, Clinician Educator, Basic Science, Clinical Practice) are institutional career tracks within this fellowship, not separate physician specialties. The extra one-year Johns Hopkins Glomerular Diseases Fellowship is a distinct advanced institutional fellowship opportunity; the one-year Transplant Nephrology Fellowship is separately listed, complementary and separately accredited by ASN/AST (ACGME transplant requirements effective 2025); neither is merged into this general program. Hopkins describes a possible NIH-collaborative critical care-nephrology career path, not a separately verified combined board or distinct general fellowship variant. Bioengineering, clinical pharmacology, global health, research degrees and education routes are supplements, not nephrology boards or separate specialties. No pediatric nephrology track is asserted. No nonphysician category is included.

practiceQuestions.stem: A stable outpatient has eGFR values below 60 mL/min/1.73m² on tests 5 weeks apart. What is the strongest inference from these two measurements alone?

options.text: CKD is established because both values are low.
The data show reduced kidney function but do not yet establish the required chronicity interval.
Dialysis is indicated.
The underlying cause is diabetic kidney disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO CKD defines chronicity using evidence persisting at least 3 months; two results five weeks apart do not alone establish chronicity or etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with AKI has a new potassium result flagged high, but the specimen is hemolyzed and the patient has no corroborating ECG or repeat result. Which interpretation best reflects safe reasoning?

options.text: Assume true severe hyperkalemia and diagnose intrinsic AKI.
Consider pseudohyperkalemia and urgently verify/assess clinically as appropriate; the initial specimen alone is limited.
Exclude hyperkalemia because there are no ECG changes.
Treat the potassium result as proof of a specific tubular disorder.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM blueprint includes pseudohyperkalemia among potassium disorders; hemolysis is a specimen limitation, not proof that potassium is normal. The item is educational and not a real-patient directive.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which combination is most appropriate for initial characterization of possible CKD risk under KDIGO 2024?

options.text: Serum creatinine alone, without urine testing.
Cause, GFR category and albuminuria category considered together.
Kidney size alone.
Dialysis status only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO 2024 uses cause-GFR-albuminuria (CGA) classification and risk assessment, with clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A new creatinine rise appears after hypotension and exposure to a nephrotoxic drug. Urine sediment is not yet reviewed. Which statement is best?

options.text: A single cause is already proven.
Hemodynamic and parenchymal mechanisms may coexist; chronology, volume/hemodynamics, sediment, medication context and obstruction assessment inform the differential.
This proves a primary glomerulonephritis.
RRT is automatically required.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AKI has multiple etiologic categories, and multifactorial injury is possible. KDIGO update status should be checked: the 2012 published guideline remains posted while a 2026 draft update was under public review.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a patient with hypotonic hyponatremia, why is serum tonicity established before classifying the disorder?

options.text: To distinguish true hypotonicity from hypertonic or isotonic/pseudohyponatremia contexts.
Because tonicity determines the histologic diagnosis.
To infer chronicity from a single sodium value.
To calculate GFR.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM blueprint explicitly separates hypotonic, hypertonic and isotonic/pseudohyponatremia and emphasizes osmolality-based reasoning.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case shows metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Which conclusion is appropriate at this stage?

options.text: Renal tubular acidosis is certain.
Consider renal tubular acidosis and nonrenal bicarbonate loss among alternatives; use potassium, urine and clinical context to discriminate.
The patient has lactic acidosis.
No renal evaluation is needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Normal-anion-gap acidosis has renal and nonrenal causes; ABIM blueprint includes RTA and nonrenal causes. No single lab pattern here is pathognomonic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person with CKD is considering kidney replacement choices. Which course conclusion is supported?

options.text: Hemodialysis is the only valid pathway.
Compare modalities, transplant and conservative management using patient priorities, clinical context, access and shared decision-making.
A lecture course can select the modality.
Start dialysis based only on eGFR.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO and NIDDK emphasize individualized care; ABIM blueprint covers dialysis modalities and initiation/discontinuation. This fictional educational item does not prescribe care.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most defensible way to interpret the 2026 KDIGO AKI guideline page?

options.text: The 2026 update is final and supersedes the 2012 guideline.
The page states a 2026 draft was released for public review; the published 2012 guideline remains linked pending final update.
No AKI guideline exists.
Guideline publication proves every recommendation is high certainty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The KDIGO AKI page reports the draft was under preparation following public review and links the published 2012 guideline. Distinguish draft from final guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation of a kidney transplant with graft dysfunction and hematuria in a linked teaching case?

options.text: Recurrent IgA nephropathy must be the sole explanation.
Maintain a differential including recurrent disease, rejection, infection, obstruction and other context-specific causes; the cited Radiopaedia case itself had more than one pathologic finding.
Imaging alone proves rejection.
No further context is needed.

assignment.title: Transplant consult reasoning and evidence brief
assignment.instructions: For a fictional adult kidney-recipient scenario supplied by the instructor, prepare (1) a time-ordered differential for graft dysfunction, (2) a data and consultation plan that names what is known and unknown, (3) a paragraph mapping one biopsy or viral result to current Banff/KDIGO/consensus guidance, and (4) a patient-facing explanation of uncertainty. rubric.differential (30%): Covers hemodynamic, structural, drug, immune, infection and recurrent/de novo possibilities with timing rationale.
rubric.evidence (25%): Uses a current primary guideline/reference and distinguishes guideline from local policy.
rubric.uncertainty (20%): Does not overinterpret isolated creatinine, DSA, viral load, stain or pathology score.
rubric.communication (15%): Clear respectful explanation, shared decisions, equity and privacy.
rubric.safety (10%): Names supervising transplant team and limits; no unsupervised treatment/procedure claims.

topicGaps: 36-hour specialty-specific free-video target remains unfilled: actual gap is 24.656111 hours; only observed-duration, unique public recordings count.

Candidate evaluation, allocation policy, health-equity decision-making and social/psychosocial assessment still lack a broad verified full-length specialty lecture sequence; the intro script is planned, not a recording.

Living-donor GFR is covered by two existing older specialty lectures and preserved KDIGO reading; donor autonomy, genetic risk, donor outcomes and full program evaluation remain incomplete in counted recordings.

HLA, SAB, cPRA, CDC/flow and virtual-crossmatch coverage improves with one current 2025 AST webinar, but detailed laboratory interpretation, unacceptable-antigen policy, paired exchange and desensitization remain incomplete; current center/lab policy controls.
Perioperative management, induction, delayed graft function, dialysis, vascular/obstructive complications and surgical escalation remain underrepresented in counted dedicated videos.

Biopsy and Banff coverage improves with the existing AMR/pathology videos and the AST/ISOT biomarker webinar, but TCMR, current Banff subcategories, chronic lesions, recurrent disease and pathology-led visual interpretation need more current structured teaching.

BK and CMV have existing lectures, but breadth remains insufficient for infection risk, prevention, resistance, donor-derived disease and pediatric infection; pair older videos with the 2024 BK and 2025 CMV consensus documents.
Long-term cardiometabolic, bone, hematologic, malignancy, reproductive/vaccine, pediatric, pancreas, multiorgan, QAPI and patient-reported outcome topics remain underrepresented in counted videos.

Failing-graft transition has a newly verified 2023 webinar, but time-sensitive OPTN wait-time restoration policy, dialysis transition, immunosuppression decisions, retransplantation and supportive care still require current primary guidance and local expertise.
No separate transplant-nephrology board examination or dedicated exam blueprint was identified; related domains remain mapped to ABIM Nephrology and ACGME competencies only.

boardStatus.transplantNephrologyBoardExam: No separate ABMS/ABIM Transplant Nephrology certificate or exam was identified in the current published ABMS certificate list or ABIM subspecialty policy pages checked 2026-10-07. This is a checked absence, not a guarantee about every non-ABMS credential.
boardStatus.relatedBoard: ABIM administers Nephrology certification; separate general-nephrology eligibility and training rules apply. Transplant fellowship completion alone does not establish eligibility.
boardStatus.blueprint: No separate transplant-nephrology exam blueprint identified. Units map to published ACGME transplant-nephrology competencies and adjacent general ABIM Nephrology concepts; this is not an official transplant board blueprint.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Hopkins states applicants must be board-certified or board-eligible in Internal Medicine and Nephrology by ABIM (or equivalent for an international scholar) and should have completed or be completing ACGME general nephrology fellowship or equivalent. ABIM eligibility is governed by current ABIM policy and the training program, not this course. No independent educational course confers board eligibility.

officialProgrammes.name: Transplant Nephrology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory labels accrediting body “Non-Standard,” describes one year and self-reports ASN/AST accreditation since 2003. The division page describes the one-year clinical physician fellowship and curriculum. Second official Hopkins URL for the same named program: https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/nephrology/education/transplant-fellowship.

officialProgrammes.name: Transplant Nephrology Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

programmeSourceScope.packetVariant: Only the exact Johns Hopkins School of Medicine Transplant Nephrology Fellowship appears in the supplied packet. The two Hopkins pages describe the same program, not distinct institutional variants. No Harvard offering is included in this item packet.
programmeSourceScope.actualPhysicianSpecialty: Yes: an advanced clinical physician fellowship in transplant nephrology.
programmeSourceScope.institutionTrack: Hopkins publicly describes 24 inpatient weeks, outpatient training, HLA/tissue-typing, selection meetings, brief liver or lung service rotation and optional renal pathology elective. Its page lists 30 outpatient recipients longitudinally, 25 potential recipient evaluations and 10 potential living donor evaluations. These are institutional-page claims, not independent verification or this course’s case-volume promise.
programmeSourceScope.combinedProgramme: No distinct combined degree or board program identified. Multiorgan consults and brief exposure are curriculum elements, not a separate combined-organ fellowship.
programmeSourceScope.directoryCategory: The Hopkins Fellowship Directory says “Non-Standard,” one year and ASN/AST accreditation since 2003, complementary to ACGME general nephrology. That label does not mean the transplant fellowship itself is ACGME-accredited.
programmeSourceScope.ACGMEStatus: ACGME published transplant-nephrology requirements effective 2025, including a 12-month program and minimum six months inpatient; AST describes the transition/application timeline. The Hopkins pages checked 2026-10-07 still disclose ASN/AST accreditation and a Non-Standard directory label; no Hopkins-specific public ACGME initial-accreditation confirmation was located. Current Hopkins-specific ACGME status remains unverified. Hopkins reports 24 inpatient weeks, while ACGME requires at least six months; possible page staleness or standard difference is unresolved.
programmeSourceScope.researchOrNonPhysicianSupplement: Hopkins describes optional transplant-related research beyond the one-year clinical fellowship. It is separate from the clinical training, not a physician specialty or board exam. No non-physician track is included.

sourceCaveats: Hopkins pages are program self-descriptions. Its specific current ACGME accreditation status could not be confirmed in an accessible public program-specific source.

The 2025 ACGME transplant-nephrology requirements, Hopkins 24-week public inpatient statement and historical ASN/AST accreditation label refer to different standards/time points; reconcile with the program before relying on current accreditation status.
No separate ABMS transplant-nephrology board examination or dedicated blueprint was found. ABIM Nephrology certification is a related, separate credential and requires its own training/eligibility.
The 2009 KDIGO recipient summary and several free lectures are historical. Current Banff, BK, CMV, OPTN and local program policy must take precedence where updated.
YouTube duration and access observations are snapshots taken 2026-10-07. Videos may be removed, region-restricted or changed; recheck before assignment. No login was used.
The UTHSC AST 25-core-lecture page is a topic syllabus, not 25 publicly evidenced recordings or known didactic hours.
Program-reported transplant counts/clinic case requirements were not converted into educational case-volume promises.
Clinical recommendations have not undergone human transplant-nephrology review.

unknownDurationItems.title: ISN-KDIGO Webinar: Management of the Patient with a Failing Kidney Allograft
unknownDurationItems.reason: Accessible duration not structurally supported by evidence.

topicGaps: 36-hour specialty-specific free-video target remains unfilled: actual gap is 24.656111 hours; only observed-duration, unique public recordings count.

Candidate evaluation, allocation policy, health-equity decision-making and social/psychosocial assessment still lack a broad verified full-length specialty lecture sequence; the intro script is planned, not a recording.

Living-donor GFR is covered by two existing older specialty lectures and preserved KDIGO reading; donor autonomy, genetic risk, donor outcomes and full program evaluation remain incomplete in counted recordings.

HLA, SAB, cPRA, CDC/flow and virtual-crossmatch coverage improves with one current 2025 AST webinar, but detailed laboratory interpretation, unacceptable-antigen policy, paired exchange and desensitization remain incomplete; current center/lab policy controls.
Perioperative management, induction, delayed graft function, dialysis, vascular/obstructive complications and surgical escalation remain underrepresented in counted dedicated videos.

Biopsy and Banff coverage improves with the existing AMR/pathology videos and the AST/ISOT biomarker webinar, but TCMR, current Banff subcategories, chronic lesions, recurrent disease and pathology-led visual interpretation need more current structured teaching.

BK and CMV have existing lectures, but breadth remains insufficient for infection risk, prevention, resistance, donor-derived disease and pediatric infection; pair older videos with the 2024 BK and 2025 CMV consensus documents.
Long-term cardiometabolic, bone, hematologic, malignancy, reproductive/vaccine, pediatric, pancreas, multiorgan, QAPI and patient-reported outcome topics remain underrepresented in counted videos.

Failing-graft transition has a newly verified 2023 webinar, but time-sensitive OPTN wait-time restoration policy, dialysis transition, immunosuppression decisions, retransplantation and supportive care still require current primary guidance and local expertise.
No separate transplant-nephrology board examination or dedicated exam blueprint was identified; related domains remain mapped to ABIM Nephrology and ACGME competencies only.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A kidney recipient has a persistent, otherwise unexplained increase in serum creatinine. Which approach best reflects guideline-based evaluation?

options.text: Diagnose acute rejection from creatinine alone and treat immediately.

Review trends, medications and clinical context; assess for structural/obstructive causes and relevant virologic/immunologic contributors, then seek allograft biopsy for unexplained persistent dysfunction when appropriate.
Assume calcineurin toxicity because the patient takes tacrolimus.
Repeat serum creatinine in six months before investigating.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A creatinine rise is nonspecific. KDIGO recommends biopsy for persistent unexplained increase; evaluation integrates clinical, imaging, laboratory and pathology data. This educational sequence is not a patient-specific order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A stable kidney recipient is six months post-transplant and has no BK DNAemia. Under the 2024 international consensus, which routine plasma BK screening schedule is recommended?

options.text: Monthly through month 9, then every 3 months until 2 years post-transplant.
Only if serum creatinine rises.
Daily for life.
No screening is recommended.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 consensus recommends regular plasma screening monthly through month 9, then every 3 months until 2 years after transplant; local pathways and individual contexts still matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A donor is CMV seropositive and the kidney recipient is seronegative. How should this combination be classified for post-transplant CMV risk?

options.text: Low risk, D−/R−.
High risk, D+/R−.
Intermediate risk, D−/R+.
Risk cannot be considered from serostatus.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 consensus classifies D+/R− as high risk; kidney recipients in this group are recommended prophylaxis for six months. Decisions should follow current center protocol and patient-specific circumstances.

practiceQuestions.stem: A potential living kidney donor has confirmed GFR 74 mL/min/1.73 m². What does the 2017 KDIGO donor guideline say?

options.text: This result alone automatically excludes donation.
This result alone automatically approves donation.
Approval should be individualized using demographic/health profile and the transplant program’s acceptable risk threshold.
Use serum creatinine alone and ignore measured GFR.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO describes 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m² as an individualized decision, while ≥90 is generally acceptable and <60 should not donate under that guideline. Risk and local policy require expert assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A kidney biopsy has microvascular inflammation. Which statement best reflects Banff active AMR criteria?

options.text: Microvascular inflammation alone always establishes active AMR.
Diagnosis integrates qualifying active lesions, evidence of antibody-endothelial interaction, and DSA evidence; C4d may substitute for DSA in specified criteria.
Negative C4d excludes every form of AMR.
A positive DSA without biopsy context always establishes rejection.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Banff requires integration of three criteria and lists important contexts where MVI alone is insufficient; C4d can substitute for DSA under defined conditions. Always use current live Banff criteria and pathology consultation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A recipient has sustained plasma BK DNAemia. Which principle is supported by the 2024 consensus?

options.text: Change assays and specimen types at every draw to increase sensitivity.
Use the same specimen type and assay where possible and monitor viral kinetics; reduction of maintenance immunosuppression is the primary intervention for sustained DNAemia.
Start an antiviral drug proven to eradicate BK in all patients.
Ignore possible rejection risk when immunosuppression changes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The consensus recommends consistent specimen/assay for comparable viral trends; reduction in immunosuppression is the primary management strategy, balanced against rejection risk with transplant-team oversight. No effective approved BK antiviral is established as universal treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult transplant candidate has a history of missed medications during depression, now improved with counseling. Which approach aligns with KDIGO and OPTN ethics guidance?

options.text: Permanently exclude the candidate for any past missed dose.
Assess barriers, offer support and counseling, and individualize the decision rather than treating past nonadherence as an automatic exclusion.
Require a specific family structure regardless of functional support needs.
Use immigration status as the decisive candidacy criterion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO recommends assessing barriers and offering adherence support; a history alone should not categorically exclude except ongoing health-compromising nonadherence despite education/counseling. OPTN ethics guidance emphasizes equitable, transparent assessment; immigration status alone should not determine candidacy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A kidney transplant recipient has rising BK DNAemia, stable creatinine and high immunologic risk. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: A biopsy is always mandatory immediately regardless of clinical context.
Interpret viral kinetics with the same assay and clinical risk; biopsy decisions depend on graft function, immunologic/virologic risk and whether histology would affect management.
BK DNAemia proves biopsy-proven nephropathy.
A positive urine test alone establishes rejection.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Consensus guidance couples virologic testing with function and immunologic context. A positive BK test does not prove tissue disease or rejection; biopsy use is context dependent.

practiceQuestions.stem: A kidney recipient with CMV DNAemia is being followed in one laboratory. Which monitoring practice improves interpretation?

options.text: Switch between plasma and whole blood without documenting the change.
Consistently use one specimen type and interpret results with assay-specific context and clinical status.
Use CMV IgM as the sole post-transplant viral-load measure.
Assume a single negative quantitative test excludes future disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 consensus notes that specimen types yield different quantitative results and recommends consistency when monitoring; CMV QNAT is interpreted with clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational board-style question asks whether age alone is a reason to reject a kidney transplant candidate. Which answer best reflects KDIGO?

options.text: Yes, because age alone is a contraindication.
No; consider age in context of comorbidities and frailty rather than excluding on age alone.
Only chronological age determines post-transplant benefit.
Candidate evaluation is unnecessary if dialysis has started.

practiceQuestions.rationale: KDIGO advises not to exclude candidates on age alone; assess comorbidities including frailty, relevant outcomes and individual context.

title: Adult Neurology Residency Program

prerequisites.level: Advanced medical learner or physician self-study; designed for learners who have completed core human anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology and basic neurologic examination.
priorKnowledge: Clinical history taking and general physical examination
Basic interpretation of laboratory tests and CT/MRI reports
prerequisites.limits: This is independent educational content, not a medical degree or supervised GME. Viewers must not apply it as unsupervised patient-care, procedural, prescribing or emergency-response instruction.

objectives: Represent neurologic symptoms by tempo, syndrome and functional impact.
Localize lesions from history and examination while keeping alternative explanations explicit.
Select diagnostic tests by clinical question and explain test limitations.
Recognize adult neurologic emergencies requiring immediate qualified clinical evaluation.
Compare major ABPN Neurology certification domains with a personal self-study plan.
Appraise current authoritative guidelines, version dates and population limits.
Communicate uncertainty, safety concerns and handoffs with respect for patient autonomy and privacy.
Distinguish the Johns Hopkins adult clinical residency from child neurology, combined training and research-only categories.

units.title: Clinical reasoning, neuroanatomy and localization
objectives: Build a concise time course and syndrome representation from a history and neurologic examination.
Localize lesions across cortex, subcortical structures, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, root, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle.
Use localization to choose focused tests and retain a differential rather than anchor on an incidental scan finding.
topics: Neurologic history and examination
Neuroanatomical localization
Temporal profile and localization-to-etiology method
Cognitive bias and test stewardship
units.casePractice: Use a fictional pattern-recognition vignette without patient images; articulate localization, time course, and two competing causes.
units.assessment: One-page localization map scored using the analytic rubric.

units.title: Vascular neurology and transient focal syndromes
objectives: Distinguish vascular-territory syndromes and common mimics using onset, exam and imaging context.
Explain the urgency of stroke-system evaluation and use a current protocol as the governing treatment source.
Interpret the limits of public educational references and avoid treatment decisions from an online course.
topics: Ischemic stroke and TIA
Intracerebral/subarachnoid hemorrhage
Cerebral venous thrombosis, dissection, vasculopathy
Secondary prevention and systems of care
units.casePractice: Compare public Radiopaedia ischemic stroke cases via source links only; identify pattern and limitations.
units.assessment: Stroke vignette: timing/territory differential and safe escalation map; no drug/dose order.

units.title: Epilepsy, episodic events and EEG reasoning
objectives: Classify a transient event from witness history and semiology while considering syncope and functional events.
Describe how EEG and imaging answer particular diagnostic questions and where they can mislead.
Recognize that status epilepticus is an emergency requiring locally governed pathways.
topics: Focal/generalized seizure patterns
Syncope, migraine and other mimics
EEG principles, status and seizure safety
Epilepsy diagnosis and counseling
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional witness account and create a semiology-based differential; no proprietary EEG traces.
units.assessment: Short structured differential with what additional test would change the working model.

units.title: Headache, neuro-ophthalmology and vestibular neurology
objectives: Separate primary headache patterns from urgent secondary-headache warning features.
Describe a focused approach to optic-disc swelling and avoid equating papilledema with any optic-disc edema.
Use history and examination to distinguish positional vertigo from central vestibular red flags.
topics: Migraine and other primary headache
Secondary headache red flags
Papilledema, optic neuropathy and visual pathways
BPPV and vestibular syndromes
units.casePractice: Describe the diagnostic question for a public case link; do not download or republish images.
units.assessment: Two oral-style explanations: headache red flags and vertigo localization.

units.title: Movement disorders and parkinsonism
objectives: Phenotype tremor, bradykinesia, dystonia, chorea, myoclonus and ataxia.
Recognize emergency syndromes and medication-related mimics that merit urgent supervised evaluation.
Distinguish Parkinson disease from atypical parkinsonism without overstating certainty.
topics: Parkinson disease and parkinsonism
Tremor, dystonia, chorea, tic and ataxia
Movement emergencies and treatment complications
Functional movement disorder positive signs
units.casePractice: Fictional phenomenology comparison in words only; no procedural training.
units.assessment: Phenomenology table and urgency rationale.

units.title: Neuromuscular disease and peripheral localization
objectives: Localize weakness to motor neuron, root, nerve, NMJ or muscle using distribution, reflexes and time course.
Interpret the role and limitations of nerve conduction studies, EMG, CK and antibody/genetic tests.
Recognize rapidly progressive weakness or respiratory/bulbar symptoms as urgent escalation features.
topics: Neuropathy, radiculopathy and plexopathy
GBS/CIDP pattern recognition
Myasthenia and other NMJ disorders
Myopathy, motor neuron disease and ALS communication/palliation
units.casePractice: Fictional localization grid; no personal medical data.
units.assessment: Explain one localization with discriminating findings and test purpose.

units.title: Neuroimmunology and demyelinating disease
objectives: Compare time course and syndrome in MS, NMOSD, MOG-associated disease, myelitis and mimics.
Explain that antibody testing and MRI are interpreted in clinical context and diagnostic criteria, not alone.
Summarize relapse/prevention concepts without prescribing or presenting dated drug choices as current.
topics: Multiple sclerosis
AQP4-positive NMOSD and MOGAD
Autoimmune encephalitis and CNS vasculitis
Demyelinating mimics and longitudinal lesion patterns
units.casePractice: Compare linked authentic MS case with source article; do not infer diagnosis from image alone.
units.assessment: Criteria-versus-mimic matrix; cite current guideline date.

units.title: Neuroinfectious disease
objectives: Classify CNS infection syndromes by localization, time course, immune status, exposure and geography.
Explain appropriate diagnostic priorities at a high level, including when a delay in emergency care is unsafe.
Maintain broad differentials and distinguish evidence in an educational case from current management guidance.
topics: Meningitis and encephalitis
Brain abscess and focal lesions
Neuroborreliosis/neurosyphilis and chronic infection
Immunocompromised host and opportunistic infections
units.casePractice: Review brain-abscess case link; identify a differential, not a definitive diagnosis from images alone.
units.assessment: Syndrome-time-course matrix with one testing caveat per branch.

units.title: Behavioral/cognitive neurology, sleep and neuropsychiatry
objectives: Differentiate cognitive domains and select collateral history and functional context.
Recognize delirium, progressive neurocognitive syndromes, sleep disorders and psychiatric overlap.
Communicate uncertainty and function-focused goals respectfully.
topics: Cognitive screening and neuropsychological reasoning
Neurodegeneration and rapidly progressive cognition
Sleep disorders and sleep history
Behavioral neurology, capacity and communication
units.casePractice: Fictional collateral-history exercise; do not record or share identifiable information.
units.assessment: Domain-based history summary and explanation of one competing diagnosis.

units.title: Neurocritical care, neuro-oncology, trauma and spinal cord
objectives: Recognize neurologic deterioration patterns that require urgent escalation.
Describe broad localization/differential for traumatic brain/spinal injury, tumor-related neurologic change and altered consciousness.
Use current local protocols and multidisciplinary decision making rather than a self-study script for acute care.
topics: Coma and neurocritical syndromes
Traumatic brain injury, spinal trauma and compression
Neuro-oncologic disorders and seizures
ICU complications, prognostication and consultation
units.casePractice: Conceptual discussion of linked cases; no imported or altered patient imaging.
units.assessment: One-page deterioration escalation map with uncertainty and team roles.

units.title: Genetic/developmental and autonomic neurology across adulthood
objectives: Recognize adult presentations that warrant family history, genetic counseling and referral.
Differentiate autonomic symptom patterns and choose a focused history/exam framework.
Avoid deterministic interpretation of genetic findings or ancestry-based assumptions.
topics: Neurogenetics and adult-onset inherited conditions
Normal development and cognitive aging relevant to adult practice
Autonomic disorders
Ethics, consent and genetic counseling boundaries
units.casePractice: Fictional pedigree with no identifiable family; list referral questions, not a genetic diagnosis.
units.assessment: Pedigree reasoning and consent/risk communication rubric.

units.title: Continuity, pregnancy, pain, rehabilitation and professional practice
objectives: Integrate safety, accessibility, life context and communication into neurologic care reasoning.
Discuss neurologic issues in pregnancy and chronic neurologic symptoms without issuing individual treatment advice.
Use evidence updates, shared decisions, rehabilitation goals, palliative care and quality improvement concepts.
topics: Cerebrovascular events in pregnancy
Neurologic health across diverse populations
Chronic pain/integrative care evidence appraisal
Rehabilitation, palliative communication, quality/safety and systems
units.casePractice: Fictional shared-decision reflection; no patient advice or real case file submission.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal and reflective handover; foundation video remains separate from specialty hours.

assignment.title: Adult Neurology Reasoning Portfolio (self-study)
deliverables: Three fictional, text-only cases: focal deficit; progressive weakness; and cognitive or episodic symptom. Do not submit real patient records, images, dates, or identifiers.
For each, state syndrome, tempo, localization, prioritized differential, what information would change the working model, and why each proposed test is relevant.
One short evidence appraisal using an up-to-date guideline page, with date checked and population/limits noted.
One reflection on uncertainty, handoff, accessibility, and where supervised clinical learning is indispensable.

rubric.2: Partially organized or conflates symptom and diagnosis.
rubric.4: Precise, neutral, separates observed findings from interpretation.

rubric.2: Plausible but narrow or weakly justified.
rubric.4: Coherent localization with alternatives and discriminating features.

rubric.2: Some test purpose but gaps in limits.
rubric.4: Each test tied to a question; limitations stated.

rubric.2: Citations present but date/safety caveat incomplete.
rubric.4: Uses current authoritative source, date-checks and clearly escalates urgent presentations.

rubric.0: Uses identifiable patient data or misleading certainty.
rubric.2: Mostly clear or privacy note incomplete.
rubric.4: Clear, respectful, uncertainty-aware, no patient identifiers.

assignment.passingInterpretation: A formative self-check only; no validated passing threshold, credential, CME or clinical competence is conferred.

methods: 12 unit objectives, retrieval checks and fictional case analyses
portfolio scored on five 0-4 rubric dimensions
self-audit against the ABPN initial certification domains and current clinical sources
assessment.limitations: Not an official ABPN examination, validated predictor, board question bank, accredited course or substitute for direct supervised evaluation.

mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official listing names Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, states ACGME Accredited and duration three years. topicGaps: Short Duke neurologic screening demonstrations now add examination examples; they do not amount to a complete specialist neurologic examination/localization course or supervised feedback.

A general adult seizure lecture is now available, but the verified set still lacks a dedicated specialist EEG-interpretation and adult status-epilepticus course; emergency decisions require current local pathways.
The added stroke-code, stroke-imaging and CT-perfusion talks expand systems and diagnostic coverage, but local protocols, current eligibility criteria and supervised team practice remain essential.

A public EDX overview and peripheral localization lecture now address the prior gap; broader electrodiagnostic sampling patterns, interpretation across NMJ/myopathy/neuropathy and case feedback remain limited.
Added myelopathy, coma, intracranial-pressure and hydrocephalus recordings improve neurocritical/spinal coverage; these are not procedural training or authorization.
Neuro-oncology, neurogenetic counseling, adult development/normal aging, psychiatric overlap and metabolic/toxic neurologic disease remain unevenly represented in counted recording coverage.
ABPN initial certification includes 20% child-neurology items; this adult curriculum intentionally leaves those domains uncovered and is not complete board preparation.
Recorded lectures do not replace repeated supervised clinical encounters, examinations, procedures or feedback; human clinical review has not been performed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) — Neurology Certification Examination (initial specialty certification)
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPN initial specialty certification examination exists. The named Johns Hopkins program page states ACGME Accredited. ABPN lists neurology subspecialty certificates separately; this course covers general adult neurology, not a fellowship certificate. The December 2025 initial certification outline specifies 80% adult and 20% child neurology items; this adult-only course does not cover the child portion and is not comprehensive preparation for the full examination. This track is not Child Neurology, Psychiatry, a combined Psychiatry-Neurology program, a research postdoctoral position, or a generic directory category.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Self-study confers no board eligibility. ABPN currently requires qualifying medical degree, applicable training (normally 12 months PGY-1 followed by 36 months in an ACGME-accredited neurology program), completion of clinical-skills evaluations, an active full unrestricted license and board application; individual pathways/policies change and must be checked with ABPN. The initial exam includes child-neurology content beyond this adult course.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Adult Neurology Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official listing names Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, states ACGME Accredited and duration three years. The department education page describes a three-year program at the two hospitals and broad exposure to inpatient, consultative and outpatient settings, but does not publish a complete rotation-by-rotation schedule or public didactic-hours inventory. ABPN training pattern places the 36-month neurology phase after PGY-1. Preserve the official Adult Neurology title; do not merge with the separate Child Neurology program.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only the packet-specified Johns Hopkins official Adult Neurology Residency is included as an institutional offering. No Harvard offering supplied in this exact task packet; none inferred. Official JH page confirms the program-specific ACGME status at date checked, superseding the packet note that requested confirmation.
sourceCaveats: The ACGME 2026 neurology requirements are effective July 1, 2026; requirements and exam criteria can change.

ABPN initial Neurology Certification Content Specifications (December 2025) are used for board mapping; the separately posted Continuing Certification outline is not substituted. The initial exam outline assigns 80% to adult and 20% to child neurology; this adult-only track intentionally does not cover the child-neurology portion and is not complete board preparation.

Johns Hopkins describes a three-year adult neurology phase. ABPN separately requires a PGY-1 year under its usual pathways. Public residency page does not publish exact elective blocks or complete curricular hours.

Public AAN playlist exposes 32 video entries; only adult-relevant substantive topics selected here are included. Pediatric-only, generic career/game-learning/fellowship information, and unspecified October webinar were excluded. One mind-body lecture is reported only as foundation time, never specialty time.
