medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has sudden right hand weakness and clear naming difficulty. Which is the best initial localization hypothesis from these data alone?

options.text: Dominant left hemispheric network, pending focused examination and confirmation.
Right peripheral ulnar nerve, because hand weakness is present.
Neuromuscular junction, because language difficulty is typical.
Cerebellar vermis, because aphasia is expected.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Aphasia with contralateral hand weakness suggests a dominant left hemispheric process, but this remains a localization hypothesis; confirm language findings and assess alternatives. A single weak hand by itself could reflect peripheral localization, but it does not explain aphasia.

practiceQuestions.stem: A first episode of transient unilateral weakness has resolved. Which reasoning step is most appropriate before concluding that it was a TIA?

options.text: Use the time course, witness history, examination and evaluation to consider vascular and nonvascular mimics.
Assume resolution proves migraine.
Assume all transient weakness is psychogenic.
Use a normal symptom-free examination to rule out vascular disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A resolved focal event still needs appropriate evaluation. Seizure, migraine, metabolic and other causes remain in the differential; resolution alone proves none of them.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes a normal early noncontrast head CT in a patient with a convincing acute focal syndrome?

options.text: It can exclude every acute ischemic stroke.
It may help evaluate hemorrhage or other structural findings, but does not exclude all early ischemia.
It establishes the stroke mechanism.
It proves a functional neurologic disorder.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A test answers a defined question; a normal early noncontrast CT does not exclude every ischemic stroke, and a scan alone does not establish the whole diagnosis or mechanism.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked to distinguish papilledema from other optic-disc edema. Which principle is most accurate?

options.text: Papilledema is a specific term and should not be used as a synonym for every swollen optic disc.
Any optic disc edema proves idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Papilledema is diagnosed from headache alone.
Disc appearance makes history and examination unnecessary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Papilledema refers to optic-disc swelling due to raised intracranial pressure; other causes of disc edema exist, so clinical evaluation and a differential remain necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which information is most helpful when classifying a transient event concerning for seizure?

options.text: Witness account, sequence of symptoms, duration, recovery and relevant context.
One normal EEG automatically excludes epilepsy.
A patient’s use of the word “spell” confirms a seizure.
A normal MRI proves syncope.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Event classification depends on semiology and context; EEG and imaging can contribute but neither single normal test automatically excludes seizure. Syncope and other mimics should be considered.

practiceQuestions.stem: A person has progressive symmetric distal sensory symptoms and absent ankle reflexes. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Localize the syndrome and characterize tempo, distribution and associated features before selecting tests.
Diagnose an inherited neuropathy without family history or testing.
Assume a spinal cord lesion because symptoms are bilateral.
Order every available test before refining the localization.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A structured peripheral localization and tempo-based differential directs focused evaluation. Bilateral symptoms are not automatically myelopathy; hereditary attribution cannot be made from this pattern alone.

practiceQuestions.stem: An MRI shows several white-matter lesions in a person with intermittent sensory symptoms. Which statement is best?

options.text: The MRI alone is sufficient to diagnose multiple sclerosis.
Interpret imaging with clinical syndrome, lesion features, appropriate diagnostic criteria and competing explanations.
Any nonspecific lesion proves NMOSD.
Clinical history is irrelevant once MRI is abnormal.

practiceQuestions.rationale: White-matter lesions have a differential. Diagnosis relies on clinical context and relevant criteria, not a nonspecific scan alone; mimics must be considered.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a patient with acute fever, headache and altered mental status, what is the safest general educational principle?

options.text: Use a course outline to select outpatient follow-up.
Recognize a potentially urgent CNS syndrome and ensure prompt evaluation by qualified clinicians using current local protocols.
Wait for a complete differential before escalation.
Assume meningitis and encephalitis can always be separated at bedside.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute CNS infection and encephalitis may be urgent. A learning resource should not delay real evaluation; syndrome boundaries can overlap and require professional investigation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which clue is a reason to consider atypical parkinsonism rather than uncomplicated idiopathic Parkinson disease?

options.text: A pattern of early severe autonomic dysfunction or early falls, which requires careful differential assessment.
Any tremor proves Parkinson disease.
Response to any medication proves the specific pathology.
A single normal examination excludes movement disorder.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Early severe autonomic dysfunction, early falls or other atypical features can prompt reconsideration of the differential, but no single clue alone establishes a specific diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A resident reviews an online AAN lecture and a dated board outline. Which practice is most appropriate before using a clinical recommendation?

options.text: Check a current authoritative guideline and local protocol, and seek qualified supervision for patient care.
Assume any lecture remains current indefinitely.
Use continuing-certification specifications as an exact replacement for the initial-certification outline.
Treat this independent course as accredited residency credit.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical recommendations change; check current sources and local protocols. Initial and continuing board outlines are different documents, and self-study is not accredited GME or exam eligibility.

Use chronology to frame DLB versus Parkinson disease dementia without relying on a single clue.
Recognize potential neuroleptic sensitivity and balance treatment discussion with uncertainty.
topics: Fluctuation, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, spontaneous parkinsonism
Attention/executive/visuospatial profile; indicative versus supportive biomarkers
DLB/PDD timing convention and mixed pathology caveats
boardDomains: Neurodegenerative disorders: Lewy body disease and related cognitive syndromes (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional patient with visuospatial deficits, fluctuating attention, hallucinations and parkinsonism; distinguish core features from tests.
units.assessment: Criteria matrix; rubric: clinical-feature classification 40%, biomarker distinction 25%, differential 20%, medication-risk awareness 15%.

units.title: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration, PPA, and language/behavior phenotypes
objectives: Distinguish behavioral-variant FTD from primary psychiatric presentations using longitudinal change and neurologic evidence.
Contrast semantic, nonfluent/agrammatic and logopenic language profiles at a high level.
Explain limits of clinical phenotype in inferring pathology or genotype.
topics: Behavioral disinhibition, apathy/inertia, loss of empathy, compulsivity, hyperorality and executive change
Primary progressive aphasia variants; motor-neuron overlap and atypical syndromes
Genetic/familial history and counseling referral; psychiatric prodrome differential
boardDomains: Neurodegenerative disorders: frontotemporal and language-led syndromes (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Use the linked FTD grand rounds as a case-discussion resource; do not reproduce its patient images or assume older claims remain current.
units.assessment: Syndrome comparison chart and written differential; rubric: phenotype 35%, competing psychiatric/medical explanations 25%, appropriate testing/referral 20%, uncertainty 20%.

units.title: Vascular cognitive impairment, mixed disease, and structural pattern reading
objectives: Connect vascular burden, temporal course and cognitive phenotype without over-attributing causality.
Describe common MRI pattern questions at a conceptual level without substituting for radiology training.
Account for mixed pathologies and vascular comorbidity.
topics: Stepwise versus gradual/insidious course; strategic infarct and small-vessel disease
MRI/CT role, lesion burden, atrophy pattern and incidental findings
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy and vascular-neurodegenerative overlap
boardDomains: Vascular and other cognitive disorders; neuroimaging interpretation (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional report summary: confluent white-matter disease plus hippocampal atrophy. State what can/cannot be inferred.
units.assessment: Imaging-to-clinical correlation memo; rubric: cautious pattern description 40%, etiologic integration 30%, avoids causal overreach 20%, readable handoff 10%.

units.title: Neuropsychiatric symptoms, affect, sleep, and behavior
objectives: Assess mood, psychosis, apathy, disinhibition, agitation and sleep symptoms in context of cognition and medical status.
Use phenomenology, timeline, collateral and function to distinguish primary psychiatric disease from neurologic causes.
Formulate nonpharmacologic/environmental strategies as discussion topics and identify urgent safety concerns.
topics: Depression/anxiety, apathy, psychosis, agitation, emotional lability, anosognosia
Sleep/wake and REM sleep behavior symptoms
Care-partner perspective; risk, capacity, consent and medication adverse effects
boardDomains: Neuropsychiatric manifestations and behavioral management (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional new paranoia with fluctuating alertness: distinguish chronic symptom formulation from acute medical change.
units.assessment: Behavioral formulation and safety handoff; rubric: phenomenology 25%, differential 25%, reversible/urgent causes 25%, respectful communication 25%.

units.title: Other syndromes and rapidly progressive cognitive change
objectives: Recognize when movement, language, visuospatial, prion, autoimmune, infectious, seizure or systemic disease changes the differential.
Identify rapid progression as a prompt for timely specialist/urgent evaluation.
Avoid anchoring on common degenerative diagnoses.
topics: Corticobasal syndrome, PSP, Huntington disease, NPH, CJD and autoimmune encephalitis overview
Subacute course and red flags; MRI/EEG/CSF/laboratory choices depend on clinical setting
Age, exposures, medication and neurologic exam as discriminators
boardDomains: Other neurologic and neuropsychiatric disorders causing cognitive/behavioral syndromes (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional weeks-long cognitive/behavioral decline with myoclonus: formulate why routine outpatient dementia pathway alone is insufficient.
units.assessment: Urgency/differential flowchart; rubric: rapid-course recognition 40%, broad differential 25%, reasoned tests 25%, avoids diagnosis certainty 10%.

units.title: Biomarkers, genetics, and test interpretation
objectives: Match biomarker tests to a clinical question and pretest context.
Interpret assay performance, sensitivity/specificity and predictive value without treating a positive test as a complete diagnosis.
Apply 2025 Alzheimer Association BBM recommendations within their specified symptomatic specialty-care scope.
topics: MRI, FDG-PET, amyloid/tau PET, CSF and emerging plasma p-tau/Aβ tests
2025 guideline: ≥90% sensitivity/≥75% specificity triage; ≥90%/≥90% confirmatory substitute conditions, only in applicable specialty setting; actual assay validation matters
Genetic risk versus diagnosis; counseling and disclosure
boardDomains: Diagnostic testing, biomarkers and genetics (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional symptomatic referral with an unspecified commercial plasma test; request assay-specific performance and interpret with context, not alone.
units.assessment: Two-page biomarker note; rubric: population/scope 30%, performance metrics 30%, contextual interpretation 25%, ethical communication 15%.

units.title: Management principles, safety, and interprofessional care
objectives: Summarize a person-centered care plan across cognition, behavior, function, caregiver needs and safety.
Identify medication review, comorbidity, function, driving/home safety and follow-up as domains for supervised clinical care.
Critically appraise changing disease-modifying claims against current authoritative sources.
topics: Shared decision-making and care-partner support
Symptom-directed treatment evidence/risks; DLB antipsychotic sensitivity; no individualized prescribing
Current labels/guidelines, monitoring and adverse events; do not infer eligibility from this course
boardDomains: Treatment, counseling, safety and longitudinal care (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional family conference: list questions and multidisciplinary referrals, not medication orders.
units.assessment: Care-plan outline; rubric: person-centered goals 25%, safety 25%, evidence currency 25%, role boundaries 25%.

units.title: Ethics, capacity, disclosure, research literacy, and board synthesis
objectives: Communicate syndrome, likely disease, uncertainty and next steps sensitively.
Distinguish decisional capacity from diagnosis and legal competence; identify jurisdictional limits.
Apply integrative reasoning to a case and identify actual UCNS examination logistics/eligibility using current official sources.
topics: Capacity as decision/time-specific; consent, driving, finances, advance planning, genetic implications
Diagnostic disclosure and care-partner communication
Research and case ethics; exam format versus actual eligibility; synthesis and knowledge gaps
boardDomains: Ethics, counseling, clinical integration and professional practice (provisional topic mapping)
units.casePractice: Fictional patient with discordant self/care-partner account and biomarker question: practice neutral, compassionate disclosure.
units.assessment: Capstone oral-board-style case (original, not official exam); rubric: summary 20%, differential 20%, investigations 20%, communication/ethics 20%, caveats/next steps 20%.

assignment.title: Longitudinal cognitive-behavioral case formulation portfolio
assignment.description: For three fictional cases (amnestic gradual, behavior/language-led, and acute-on-chronic confusion), create a one-page problem representation, functional staging, prioritized differential, question-driven evaluation plan, uncertainty-aware communication paragraph and reflection on what would require supervised clinical judgment. No private clinical records or patient images.

unitMap.text: Cognitive-behavioral neuroanatomy and localization
coveredTopics: Frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital and limbic networks
Language, memory, visuospatial, executive and social-cognitive systems
Lateralization, disconnection, reserve and network degeneration

unitMap.text: Neurobehavioral examination and neuropsychological assessment
coveredTopics: Mental status and focused neurologic examination
Memory encoding/retrieval, naming, fluency, visuospatial/executive and social cognition
MoCA/MMSE limitations, language/culture/education, effort and functional corroboration

unitMap.text: Syndrome formulation, delirium, and reversible contributors
coveredTopics: Onset and trajectory; functional independence; collateral history
Delirium, mood/sleep, medication effects, metabolic/endocrine/nutritional causes, structural disease
Rapidly progressive dementia red flags and escalation

unitMap.text: Alzheimer disease and amnestic cognitive syndromes
coveredTopics: Episodic memory phenotype, MCI/dementia functional threshold, atypical presentations
Mixed pathology, structural imaging and biomarker interpretation
Current DETeCD-ADRD specialty evaluation; anti-amyloid therapy only as an evidence/label-safety discussion, not a treatment protocol

unitMap.text: Lewy body disease and Parkinson disease cognitive/behavioral syndromes
coveredTopics: Fluctuation, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, spontaneous parkinsonism
Attention/executive/visuospatial profile; indicative versus supportive biomarkers
DLB/PDD timing convention and mixed pathology caveats

unitMap.text: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration, PPA, and language/behavior phenotypes
coveredTopics: Behavioral disinhibition, apathy/inertia, loss of empathy, compulsivity, hyperorality and executive change
Primary progressive aphasia variants; motor-neuron overlap and atypical syndromes
Genetic/familial history and counseling referral; psychiatric prodrome differential

unitMap.text: Vascular cognitive impairment, mixed disease, and structural pattern reading
coveredTopics: Stepwise versus gradual/insidious course; strategic infarct and small-vessel disease
MRI/CT role, lesion burden, atrophy pattern and incidental findings
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy and vascular-neurodegenerative overlap

unitMap.text: Neuropsychiatric symptoms, affect, sleep, and behavior
coveredTopics: Depression/anxiety, apathy, psychosis, agitation, emotional lability, anosognosia
Sleep/wake and REM sleep behavior symptoms
Care-partner perspective; risk, capacity, consent and medication adverse effects

unitMap.text: Other syndromes and rapidly progressive cognitive change
coveredTopics: Corticobasal syndrome, PSP, Huntington disease, NPH, CJD and autoimmune encephalitis overview
Subacute course and red flags; MRI/EEG/CSF/laboratory choices depend on clinical setting
Age, exposures, medication and neurologic exam as discriminators

unitMap.text: Biomarkers, genetics, and test interpretation
coveredTopics: MRI, FDG-PET, amyloid/tau PET, CSF and emerging plasma p-tau/Aβ tests
2025 guideline: ≥90% sensitivity/≥75% specificity triage; ≥90%/≥90% confirmatory substitute conditions, only in applicable specialty setting; actual assay validation matters
Genetic risk versus diagnosis; counseling and disclosure

unitMap.text: Management principles, safety, and interprofessional care
coveredTopics: Shared decision-making and care-partner support
Symptom-directed treatment evidence/risks; DLB antipsychotic sensitivity; no individualized prescribing
Current labels/guidelines, monitoring and adverse events; do not infer eligibility from this course

unitMap.text: Ethics, capacity, disclosure, research literacy, and board synthesis
coveredTopics: Capacity as decision/time-specific; consent, driving, finances, advance planning, genetic implications
Diagnostic disclosure and care-partner communication
Research and case ethics; exam format versus actual eligibility; synthesis and knowledge gaps

topicGaps: The 36-hour recorded-video floor remains unmet: 6.534444 unique free-public recorded hours are verified, leaving an actual 29.465556-hour gap. Planned episodes are not recordings and count as zero hours.

Search and full-page checks located three additional suitable open academic recordings, but no accessible free complete BNNP lecture series or sufficient long-form recordings to reach the 36-hour target; the current public recording pool is sparse relative to the specialist domain.

UCNS publicly confirms the subspecialty examination format and links its content outline and eligibility criteria, but those PDFs redirected to an authentication portal in the supplied packet; exact domain headings/weights and applicant-specific pathway remain unverified. Do not bypass the portal.

Source-backed instruction remains thin for detailed network neuroanatomy/localization, language-led syndromes, FTD/PPA distinctions and genetic counseling, vascular cognitive impairment/imaging, rapidly progressive/prion/autoimmune differentials, capacity/ethics, and current therapy/label surveillance. Existing full-length talks are selective, sometimes historical, and not comprehensive.

Four complete original written episodes are scripted/planned in the companion file; they contribute zero recorded, rendered or runtime-verified hours. Human clinician review has not been performed. The clinical fellowship, supervised patient contact, assessment and eligibility are not replaced.

Johns Hopkins identifies this two-year fellowship as UCNS-accredited and states that fellows at completion will be eligible to take the examination. topicGaps: The 36-hour recorded-video floor remains unmet: 6.534444 unique free-public recorded hours are verified, leaving an actual 29.465556-hour gap. Planned episodes are not recordings and count as zero hours.

Search and full-page checks located three additional suitable open academic recordings, but no accessible free complete BNNP lecture series or sufficient long-form recordings to reach the 36-hour target; the current public recording pool is sparse relative to the specialist domain.

UCNS publicly confirms the subspecialty examination format and links its content outline and eligibility criteria, but those PDFs redirected to an authentication portal in the supplied packet; exact domain headings/weights and applicant-specific pathway remain unverified. Do not bypass the portal.

Source-backed instruction remains thin for detailed network neuroanatomy/localization, language-led syndromes, FTD/PPA distinctions and genetic counseling, vascular cognitive impairment/imaging, rapidly progressive/prion/autoimmune differentials, capacity/ethics, and current therapy/label surveillance. Existing full-length talks are selective, sometimes historical, and not comprehensive.

Four complete original written episodes are scripted/planned in the companion file; they contribute zero recorded, rendered or runtime-verified hours. Human clinician review has not been performed. The clinical fellowship, supervised patient contact, assessment and eligibility are not replaced.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked to assess an adult with slowly progressive cognitive complaints. Which first step most directly anchors the later syndrome formulation?

options.text: Order a disease-specific biomarker before clarifying symptoms.
Establish onset, trajectory, function, medications, medical history and informant observations.
Assume the most common dementia etiology based on age.
Use a single screening score as a final diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A structured history, collateral/function and examination define the clinical problem before increasingly specialized tests; a single score or biomarker is not a complete syndrome/etiology assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional person develops marked inattention and disorientation over 36 hours after a stable year of mild forgetfulness. What is the most appropriate conceptual priority?

options.text: Reclassify the entire course as Alzheimer disease.
Evaluate promptly for delirium and acute medical/medication contributors, while establishing baseline cognition.
Defer assessment until a six-month cognitive retest.
Diagnose major neurocognitive disorder from the acute screen.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute change in attention and cognition is an urgent delirium/medical problem; distinguish it from baseline chronic impairment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has objective cognitive deficits but remains independent in everyday activities. Which formulation is best supported before further details?

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder is established.
Mild cognitive impairment may be considered; determine functional change and likely cause.
Normal aging is established.
A positive cognitive screen establishes Alzheimer pathology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The distinction hinges substantially on functional independence, and etiology requires further clinical workup.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of a brief cognitive screen in a complex behavioral presentation?

options.text: It replaces history and domain-specific assessment.
It helps characterize global impairment but is interpreted with history, education/language context, function and, when indicated, fuller neuropsychological assessment.
A normal score excludes disease.
It identifies neuropathology directly.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screeners are useful but limited; contextual and detailed assessment may be required.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: progressive dementia with recurrent visual hallucinations, documented cognitive fluctuations and spontaneous parkinsonism. Under the DLB consensus approach, these observations are best described as:

options.text: Core clinical features; diagnostic probability still depends on criteria and full evaluation.
Indicative biomarkers.
Sufficient proof of a single pathology.
Features that exclude mixed pathology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fluctuations, recurrent visual hallucinations and spontaneous parkinsonism are core clinical features; they are not biomarkers and do not prove exclusive pathology.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the DLB consensus criteria is most accurate?

options.text: Clinical features and diagnostic biomarkers are treated as identical evidence.
The criteria distinguish core/supportive clinical features from indicative/supportive biomarkers.
A screening score is an indicative biomarker.
A patient with mixed pathology cannot have a DLB phenotype.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The revised consensus distinguishes clinical features from biomarkers and weights them differently; mixed pathology can produce atypical presentations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 55-year-old develops progressive loss of empathy, disinhibition and repetitive behavior. Which next inference is most appropriate?

options.text: Behavior alone proves frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
Consider a behavioral cognitive syndrome and evaluate longitudinal course, function, neurologic/cognitive findings and psychiatric/medical alternatives.
Exclude neurodegeneration because memory is not the first complaint.
Order genetic testing without counseling or phenotyping.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The phenotype raises FTD in the differential but is not pathognomonic. A structured evaluation and alternative explanations are essential.

practiceQuestions.stem: An individual has progressive cognitive impairment and an available plasma Alzheimer biomarker assay. Under the 2025 Alzheimer Association BBM guideline summary, what is essential before ordering/interpreting it?

options.text: Use any available assay as an interchangeable diagnostic test.
Comprehensive clinical evaluation and confirm that the patient/population and assay performance fit the specialist-care recommendations.
Treat a positive result as a complete diagnosis regardless of symptoms.
Order it for population screening of asymptomatic adults.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline applies to people with objective impairment seen in specialized memory care; performance thresholds and clinical context matter. It explicitly cautions against substitution of a comprehensive evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: For the 2025 BBM recommendations summarized by the Alzheimer’s Association, which assay performance applies to a biomarker used as a confirmatory substitute for PET/CSF in the stated specialty-care population?

options.text: At least 90% sensitivity and 75% specificity.
At least 75% sensitivity and 90% specificity.
At least 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity.
No performance requirement if marketed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The summarized confirmatory-substitute threshold is ≥90% sensitivity and specificity; ≥90% sensitivity with ≥75% specificity describes the triage threshold, with positive triage results confirmed by another method.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the Johns Hopkins official fellowship page say about programme outcome and certification?

options.text: It guarantees UCNS certification to anyone completing this independent online course.
The two-year UCNS-accredited clinical fellowship states its fellows will be eligible to take the UCNS BNNP certification examination at completion.
It is a non-physician research supplement with no clinical training.
It is an ABMS residency that replaces neurology/psychiatry training.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official page identifies a two-year UCNS-accredited fellowship and says fellows at the end of training will be eligible to take the examination. This does not grant eligibility through independent study.

title: Epilepsy Fellowship
prerequisites: Physician-level prior medical education and completed or expected ACGME-accredited adult neurology or child neurology residency are assumed for the clinical context; this course itself requires no credential and verifies none.
Basic neuroscience, clinical neurology, EEG principles, pharmacology and evidence appraisal are assumed.
Learners must not independently diagnose, read EEGs, prescribe medication, treat status epilepticus, use clinical videos outside their terms, or perform procedures based on this course.
objectives: Use the updated 2025 ILAE seizure classification and distinguish seizure type from epilepsy diagnosis, epilepsy type, syndrome and etiology.
Reason across the ABPN published epilepsy examination blueprint, including diagnostic procedures, treatment/management, neuroscience and cross-cutting competencies.
Describe EEG, video-EEG, imaging, genetics, neuropsychology and multidisciplinary presurgical evaluation concepts and their limitations.
Recognize urgent status epilepticus and suspected developmental epileptic encephalopathy as contexts for immediate supervised clinical evaluation, not self-directed care.
Communicate uncertainty, differential diagnoses, evidence and referral needs without promising candidacy or outcomes.

units.title: Clinical frame, terminology, and limits
objectives: Distinguish a seizure event, epilepsy diagnosis, seizure type, epilepsy type, syndrome, and etiology.
Use the 2025 ILAE classification concepts while identifying situations that require older terms in legacy sources.
State what independent study cannot establish about patient diagnosis or care.
topics: Clinical scope; epilepsy definition; historical/current nomenclature; adult and pediatric lifespan framing; documentation of uncertainty.
units.casePractice: Use an explicitly fictional event description and separate observation from diagnostic inference. No clinical video required.
units.assessment: Short written taxonomy exercise graded for correct level, cautious language, and identifying missing evidence.

units.title: Seizure semiology and differential of paroxysmal events
objectives: Construct a time-ordered account from a witness narrative.
Apply 2025 basic/expanded seizure classification with awareness/response-consciousness and semiologic descriptors.
Compare epileptic seizures with syncope, functional seizures, sleep and movement disorders without claiming certainty from a single sign.
topics: Focal/generalized/unknown/unclassified classes; focal and generalized semiology; mimics; event history; witness/video limitations.
units.casePractice: Use ILAE EpilepsyDiagnosis.org linked videos only after learner registration, accepting ILAE terms; no download or redistribution.
units.assessment: Vignette: time-sequence and differential worksheet; rubric rewards evidence, counterevidence, and uncertainty.

units.title: EEG fundamentals and routine EEG interpretation
objectives: Describe montage, sensitivity, artifacts, normal variants, activation, and sampling limits.
Recognize common interictal epileptiform patterns at a conceptual educational level.
Explain why normal routine EEG does not rule out epilepsy and why an EEG pattern must be contextualized.
topics: Routine and sleep EEG; artifacts; background; focal/generalized discharges; activation; reporting and limitations.
units.casePractice: Review authentic educational examples in ILAE diagnostic manual, linked and subject to its video terms; no screenshots copied.
units.assessment: Structured pattern-description practice scored for descriptive accuracy, artifact check, localization limits, and non-overclaiming.

units.title: Video-EEG monitoring, ICU EEG, and electroclinical reasoning
objectives: Explain indications and limitations of prolonged video-EEG and continuous EEG.
Integrate electroclinical evolution and artifact/context when describing a captured event.
Recognize electrographic/nonconvulsive seizure and status concepts at a supervised-learning level.
topics: EMU and continuous EEG; event capture; electroclinical correlation; ICU cEEG; electrographic seizures; artifacts; safety and monitoring teamwork.
units.casePractice: Use public education cases via ILAE clinical manual or publicly indexed EEG case conference pages; no patient records/images reproduced.
units.assessment: Mock EEG report and escalation memo; score technical caveats, clinical correlation, and clarity.

units.title: Epilepsy diagnosis, classification, etiologic work-up, and imaging
objectives: Apply epilepsy definition and multi-level ILAE diagnosis framework.
Organize structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune, and unknown etiologies.
Explain role/limits of MRI, functional imaging, genetics, and neuropsychological evaluation in multidisciplinary work-up.
topics: First/unprovoked seizure vs epilepsy; seizure/epilepsy type/syndrome; epilepsy-protocol MRI concepts; etiology and differential.
units.casePractice: Study authentic examples and diagnostic criteria through ILAE manual; use clinical images only through their source and permissions.
units.assessment: Case reasoning map graded for framework, differential, evidence selection, and missing information.

units.title: Electroclinical syndromes across the lifespan
objectives: Recognize hallmark electroclinical patterns and age ranges for common focal/generalized syndromes.
Identify developmental and epileptic encephalopathy concepts and urgency signals.
Avoid syndrome assignment where clinical, EEG, age, or etiology evidence is incomplete.
topics: Neonatal, infant, childhood, adolescent/adult syndromes; self-limited syndromes; DEE; syndrome differential.
units.casePractice: ILAE syndrome pages include genuine video examples; register directly and observe stated viewing-only conditions.
units.assessment: Syndrome comparison matrix; score pattern linking, differential and when not to label.

units.title: Pharmacotherapy principles and individualized treatment reasoning
objectives: Classify treatment evidence conceptually across seizure/epilepsy type, comorbidity, age, interactions, and reproductive context.
Explain medication selection and adverse-effect monitoring as clinician responsibilities informed by current labels/guidelines.
Distinguish seizure control, medication failure, tolerability, adherence, and diagnostic uncertainty.
topics: Antiseizure medication mechanisms; monotherapy/polytherapy reasoning; interactions; adherence; pregnancy considerations; shared decisions.
units.casePractice: Use open guideline/primary-label sources; no individualized medication or dosing recommendations in this course.
units.assessment: Compare two fictional treatment-option profiles using provided authoritative references; rubric emphasizes factors and safety checks rather than a single prescription.

units.title: Convulsive and nonconvulsive status epilepticus
objectives: Define status concepts and distinguish emergency recognition from specialist-directed treatment.
Summarize the AES evidence-based convulsive status algorithm stages at a conceptual level.
Describe escalation, EEG confirmation, causes, and team communication without instructing unsupervised care.
topics: Time-critical convulsive status; nonconvulsive status; refractory/super-refractory concepts; EEG; stabilization; etiology and protocols.
units.casePractice: Read AES open guideline and link to ILAE expert teaching; educational videos are not care protocols.

assignment.title: Fictional epilepsy case portfolio and evidence map
assignment.instructions: Create five explicitly fictional case analyses: (1) witnessed paroxysmal event with uncertain onset; (2) routine EEG and imaging limitations; (3) suspected pediatric syndrome/developmental concern; (4) drug-resistance and comprehensive-center referral question; (5) status-epilepticus evidence/communication review. For each separate observed facts, inferences, missing information, differential, board domain, source-supported reasoning, and supervised-care boundary. Use linked cases only under source terms. No copied patient data, clinical images or proprietary exam items.
deliverables: Five 400–600 word structured case-analysis worksheets
One two-page board-domain/evidence map
One current-source update log (publication date and limitations)
assignment.gradingPlan: Formative rubric: classification and clinical reasoning 30%; diagnostic evidence and limitations 25%; treatment/referral reasoning and safety boundary 20%; citation quality/currentness 15%; clear respectful communication and privacy/rights compliance 10%. No patient-care signoff or predictive board score.

topicGaps: The 36-hour verified free-recording target remains unmet: 12582 seconds (3.495000 hours) are accessible with observed runtime; residual gap is 32.505000 hours. Added recordings are unique and counted once.

Most of the examined blueprint remains without dedicated verified teaching recordings: routine EEG pattern recognition and artifacts; prolonged/ICU EEG; seizure mimics and diagnostic uncertainty; current pharmacotherapy selection and reproductive issues; status epilepticus beyond an older overview; syndrome-level pediatric/developmental epilepsy; drug resistance and referral; surgery/neuromodulation; SUDEP, psychiatric/cognitive comorbidity and systems practice.

NIH grand rounds are focused neurophysiology/research teaching rather than comprehensive clinical epilepsy curricula; the 2023 broad medical-student recording predates the 2025 ILAE seizure update and is foundational only. Neither source fills fellowship supervision, case-volume, EEG interpretation, procedural or clinical competency requirements.

Four original source-grounded episodes in the companion authored JSON are scripted, not recorded/rendered. The separate remaining-gap clip plan is production planning only, not rendered hours; additional program-specific didactic recordings are not publicly discoverable in the examined sources. Human clinician review has not been performed.

boardStatus.primaryBoard: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN)
boardStatus.status: Epilepsy is an ABPN subspecialty certification with a distinct initial certification examination. This is not a primary specialty examination. The current December 2025 content specifications describe 220 items and a two-dimensional outline.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: Dimension 1 neurologic disorders/topics: epilepsy and episodic disorders 74–86%; genetic/developmental 3–5%; other disorder categories and nonspecific topics in smaller published ranges. Dimension 2 competencies/mechanisms: diagnostic procedures and treatment/management each 31–39%, clinical aspects 17–23%, plus neuroscience and cross-cutting professionalism, communication, practice improvement, and systems-based practice. Detailed outline is linked in ABPN PDF.
boardStatus.eligibility: ABPN states candidates must have primary ABPN certification in general neurology or neurology with special qualification in child neurology, and—outside legacy practice pathway—one year of ACGME-accredited epilepsy fellowship training after residency, among other current requirements. Verify the live ABPN rules before applying.
boardStatus.institutionTrackRelationship: Hopkins states its one-year ACGME-accredited track fulfills ABPN requirements. Its optional second year is additional training, not another epilepsy board examination. The directory and department page describe accreditation of year two differently; see exact variants below.

Hopkins lists a one-year ACGME epilepsy fellowship and optional second year with accreditation wording discrepancy across its own pages. ACGME, institutional description, and ABPN exam outline are distinct sources and are labeled separately. ACGME’s 2026 general epilepsy-program standards include minimum supervised patient-care and EEG experiences (six months FTE inpatient/outpatient care, three months EEG/video-EEG; case-log FAQs specify minimum counts); these describe requirements and must not be read as Hopkins-specific case outcomes.
sourceCaveats: Hopkins department page describes a one-year ACGME-accredited and an optional ACGME-equivalent second year; Hopkins directory instead calls the second year nonaccredited. Preserve both institutional descriptions; confirm directly rather than infer accreditation.

The public Hopkins pages provide broad clinical training descriptions, not a complete public curriculum, didactic schedule, exact case volume, or lecture-duration ledger. No case-volume claim is inferred.

ABPN certification is a distinct subspecialty examination; eligibility depends on primary certification and qualifying training, not this curriculum. There is no separate epilepsy-surgery board exam claimed here.

The 2025 ILAE seizure classification update is primary for seizure type terminology; ILAE 2017 epilepsy classification page remains useful for epilepsy type/syndrome/etiology framework. Do not present the older seizure terminology as the newest classification.

YouTube video duration retrieval failed under permitted public stateless access (HTTP 429/sign-in-to-confirm-bot). No login, cookies or stateful browser was used. Two candidate lectures have unknown durations and unverified free playback and are not counted. ILAE video manual requires direct account registration and carries separate copyrighted media terms; clinical video is not board lecture-hour credit.
The ABPN content outline is a blueprint, not an official course sequence or guarantee that all outlined material is tested on any one examination.

Human clinical review is NOT PERFORMED. This independent educational curriculum grants no Hopkins/Harvard affiliation, accredited training, physician licensure, ABPN board eligibility, procedure competence, certification, or guaranteed passing.

The 2026 ACGME requirements separately call for at least six months FTE inpatient/outpatient epilepsy patient care including at least three months EEG/video-EEG monitoring; FAQs specify minimums of at least 50 routine EEGs, 20 prolonged/overnight scalp recordings as primary reviewer, and 5 intracranial recordings (including intraoperative) as primary reviewer. These are published ACGME standards, not evidence that Hopkins trainees or any learner in this course achieved those experiences.

Most of the examined blueprint remains without dedicated verified teaching recordings: routine EEG pattern recognition and artifacts; prolonged/ICU EEG; seizure mimics and diagnostic uncertainty; current pharmacotherapy selection and reproductive issues; status epilepticus beyond an older overview; syndrome-level pediatric/developmental epilepsy; drug resistance and referral; surgery/neuromodulation; SUDEP, psychiatric/cognitive comorbidity and systems practice.

NIH grand rounds are focused neurophysiology/research teaching rather than comprehensive clinical epilepsy curricula; the 2023 broad medical-student recording predates the 2025 ILAE seizure update and is foundational only. practiceQuestions.stem: A witness describes an event with possible focal onset, then bilateral convulsive movements, but cannot recall the first seconds. Which is the best classification practice under the 2025 ILAE framework?

options.text: Assign generalized onset because both sides moved.
Use available features and classify as unknown whether focal or generalized if onset cannot be determined; revise if new evidence emerges.
Diagnose psychogenic seizures from incomplete witness recall.
Call the event unclassified permanently.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Bilateral motor manifestations do not prove generalized onset. The classification is based on information available; unknown whether focal/generalized is distinct from unclassified, and classification may be revised.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has one unprovoked seizure. MRI and EEG are pending. What statement best reflects the ILAE practical definition?

options.text: One seizure always meets the definition of epilepsy.

Epilepsy may be diagnosed after one unprovoked seizure only when recurrence probability is comparable to that after two unprovoked seizures, or an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed; the pending work-up matters.
Epilepsy cannot be diagnosed until two seizures occur.
A normal examination excludes epilepsy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ILAE definition allows diagnosis after one unprovoked seizure when recurrence risk is sufficiently high (at least 60% over 10 years) or an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed; a single event alone is not automatically epilepsy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A brief routine EEG is reported as normal in a patient with convincing recurrent stereotyped events. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: A normal routine EEG rules out epilepsy.
The EEG is a time-limited sample; a normal result does not by itself exclude epilepsy.
The EEG proves the events are functional.
Repeat EEG is always mandatory.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Routine EEG sensitivity is limited by sampling and state; diagnosis remains clinical and integrated, with additional tests selected by treating clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: In the 2025 classification, a generalized-onset seizure class is distinguished from focal-onset primarily by which concept?

options.text: It must begin symmetrically in every clinical feature.
It originates within and rapidly engages bilaterally distributed networks; onset semiology may look focal or asymmetric.
It must have no EEG abnormalities.
It must include loss of consciousness.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 practical guide defines generalized seizures by rapidly engaging bilateral networks; focal-appearing features can occur.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional event includes transient loss of consciousness after prolonged standing, pallor, and rapid recovery without a clear stereotyped motor sequence. Best reasoning?

options.text: Syncope is a relevant differential; gather context and appropriate cardiovascular/neurologic evidence rather than label epilepsy from collapse alone.
This is definitely generalized epilepsy.
Rapid recovery proves functional seizures.
A single symptom is sufficient to prescribe an antiseizure medication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Syncope and anoxic events are explicitly among the ABPN paroxysmal-event differentials; history and appropriate evaluation matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has had two appropriately selected, tolerated, adequately used antiseizure medication schedules without sustained seizure freedom. What is the best educational next step?

options.text: Declare all treatments futile and stop medication.
Consider the ILAE drug-resistance definition and reassess diagnosis, adherence, appropriateness, and refer for comprehensive epilepsy evaluation when indicated.
Assume nonadherence without discussion.
Offer surgery without evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Drug resistance is based on failure of adequate medication schedules; false treatment failure should be explored, and comprehensive evaluation may be appropriate. Not a patient-specific direction.

practiceQuestions.stem: According to the 2022 ILAE expert consensus, when should evaluation for epilepsy surgery generally be offered?

options.text: Only after five medications fail.
For drug-resistant epilepsy, referral for surgical evaluation should be offered as soon as drug resistance is ascertained, subject to the consensus scope and clinician judgment.
Only if MRI shows a single lesion.
Only to adults under 30.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ILAE consensus recommends offering referral for surgical evaluation for drug-resistant epilepsy as soon as drug resistance is established; referral is not a promise of surgery or candidacy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional learner recognizes ongoing convulsive status epilepticus. Which educational action is appropriate?

options.text: Use the AES evidence-based algorithm to study the urgent care sequence, while recognizing actual treatment requires immediate supervised emergency care and local protocols.
Wait for outpatient routine EEG.
Apply a medication dose from a study question to a real person without supervision.
Assume seizures stop on their own.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Status epilepticus is time-critical; the AES guideline provides evidence-based treatment concepts, but the course is not an emergency protocol or authorization to treat.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child has developmental regression with suspected epileptic spasms. What is the safest educational framing?

options.text: Treat as a routine benign event without urgency.
Recognize possible developmental/epileptic encephalopathy and the need for urgent specialist assessment; classify only with adequate clinical and EEG information.
Diagnose one specific genetic syndrome from age alone.
Infer etiology from one video clip.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Spasms and developmental regression warrant urgent evaluation; phenotype, EEG and etiologic work-up are needed and a vignette cannot establish a specific syndrome.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which exam mapping statement is accurate?

options.text: The ABPN Epilepsy initial subspecialty exam has a single dimension limited to seizure types.
The ABPN Epilepsy initial subspecialty exam has 220 questions and a two-dimensional content outline covering disorders/topics and cross-cutting competencies/mechanisms.
There is no distinct ABPN epilepsy examination.
Passing this course grants ABPN eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current ABPN specification published December 2025 states 220 items and a two-dimensional blueprint. Independent study does not confer eligibility or certification.

topicGaps: Small-bowel and colonic transit, whole-gut transit methods, pseudo-obstruction and capsule test selection: no verified-duration new full lecture found; available evidence is not a complete teaching sequence.

Anorectal physiology, balloon expulsion, defecography, adult protocol/normal-value limits and interpretation: ANMS public webinars are relevant but full runtimes are unverified and trace reading still requires supervised training.
IBS/DGBI and functional dyspepsia: one newly mapped ANMS IBS recording has unknown runtime; substantial current, full-length instructional coverage remains absent.
Research literacy, reproducibility, diagnostic accuracy, quality reporting and cross-test discordance need broader worked instruction than the two duration-verified webinars provide.

The ABIM GI blueprint spans the general subspecialty and is not a motility-specific exam blueprint; broader GI domains and all institutional fellowship competencies cannot be inferred from the short video ledger.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (institutional one-year advanced clinical/research track; non-standard, not an ACGME-accredited GI fellowship)
boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Gastroenterology certification examination (general GI; includes motility domain; no separate motility/neurogastroenterology board exam identified)
medical.boardStatus: This is an institutional clinical/research fellowship and a generic directory category, not a physician board certification. Hopkins directory explicitly lists the program accrediting body as Non-Standard. The official department describes a one-year fellowship. The ABIM GI examination is broader; current ABIM blueprint allocates 5% to motility disorders and 6% to DGBI. No separate ABIM motility exam appears in the official list.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Hopkins states that applicants should have completed internal medicine residency and that completion of gastroenterology fellowship is desired but not mandatory. This independent self-study course does not establish eligibility for Hopkins training, ACGME training, ABIM certification, licensure or independent practice. Board eligibility is determined only by ABIM policy and accredited training/individual circumstances. ACGME general Gastroenterology programme requirement is 36 months; it is not equivalent to this one-year Non-Standard track.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / The Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Gastrointestinal Motility and Neurogastroenterology Fellowship Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Preserve exact official title. Official GI education page specifies one year; clinical and research training; procedures (HRM/impedance, pH-impedance, wireless pH, wireless capsule motility, anorectal manometry); complex achalasia, GERD, dysphagia, gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia, IBS and pelvic-floor disorders; research/conference expectation. Hopkins directory says “Accrediting Body: Non-Standard.” Eligibility page says completed IM residency; GI fellowship desired, not mandatory. Public page is not a complete syllabus or case log.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One named Johns Hopkins programme, not a Harvard variant or combined degree. The institutional directory entry is a generic fellowship-directory category, but its individual programme page describes a clinical and research physician fellowship. It is not a research-only postdoctoral appointment and not a non-physician supplement. It is separate from the ACGME-accredited 36-month general GI fellowship; do not infer ACGME accreditation from directory inclusion.
sourceCaveats: The Hopkins directory and programme page establish a one-year institutional clinical/research fellowship, not an independently accredited or board-certified motility specialty. Directory label is explicitly Non-Standard.

The public curriculum page is descriptive, not a complete syllabus or evidence of the named trainee’s procedural competence. Its expected competency language must not be transferred to self-study learners.
The 2026 ABIM GI blueprint is effective for the Fall 2026 certification exam; it is a general GI examination blueprint, not a motility-specific exam.
AGA 2025 recommendations are conditional; check the full guideline, evidence certainty and later updates before clinical application.

Public video listing runtimes were available, but YouTube metadata extraction/player playback failed in this review. Only the two surfaced full webinar durations are counted; recheck playback before course assignment.
No patient records, recordings, traces or images have been copied. Linked clinical reports are not independently audited for de-identification or image permissions.

No human clinical review was performed. Independent self-study is unaffiliated and does not replace accredited clinical training, medical education, supervised procedures, licensure, certification or board eligibility.

topicGaps: Small-bowel and colonic transit, whole-gut transit methods, pseudo-obstruction and capsule test selection: no verified-duration new full lecture found; available evidence is not a complete teaching sequence.

Anorectal physiology, balloon expulsion, defecography, adult protocol/normal-value limits and interpretation: ANMS public webinars are relevant but full runtimes are unverified and trace reading still requires supervised training.
IBS/DGBI and functional dyspepsia: one newly mapped ANMS IBS recording has unknown runtime; substantial current, full-length instructional coverage remains absent.
Research literacy, reproducibility, diagnostic accuracy, quality reporting and cross-test discordance need broader worked instruction than the two duration-verified webinars provide.

The ABIM GI blueprint spans the general subspecialty and is not a motility-specific exam blueprint; broader GI domains and all institutional fellowship competencies cannot be inferred from the short video ledger.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids. After structural evaluation, which test most directly classifies esophageal motor patterns?

options.text: High-resolution esophageal manometry
Fecal calprotectin
Four-hour gastric-emptying scintigraphy
Anorectal manometry

practiceQuestions.rationale: HRM characterizes esophageal pressure patterns; test choice depends on the clinical question and structural evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A manometry report suggests EGJ outflow obstruction. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

options.text: Any elevated IRP alone proves clinically relevant obstruction
Interpret within protocol and symptoms and seek supportive evidence where needed
Treat every such pattern as achalasia
Ignore symptoms if peristalsis is present

practiceQuestions.rationale: A single metric/pattern should not be overcalled; symptom context and supportive testing may be needed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which definition best fits gastroparesis?

options.text: Nausea with normal emptying and no evaluation
Symptoms compatible with food retention plus objective delayed emptying without mechanical obstruction
Any delayed emptying regardless of symptoms or obstruction
Postprandial fullness alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACG definition requires compatible symptoms, objective delay and absence of mechanical obstruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: For suspected gastroparesis, the 2025 AGA guideline suggests which test duration compared with a shorter study?

options.text: A 30-minute study
A 2-hour study only
A 4-hour study rather than a 2-hour-or-shorter study
No emptying assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: AGA suggests against a 2-hour or shorter study compared with a 4-hour study; this is conditional guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient’s gastric emptying is delayed on a technically shortened study while taking motility-altering medication. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Definitive idiopathic gastroparesis
Protocol and medication context may confound the finding; clarify validity before etiologic claims
The symptoms are necessarily functional
Immediate pyloric intervention is indicated

practiceQuestions.rationale: Interpret the protocol and confounders, and avoid concluding etiology from one compromised measurement.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with IBS-D symptoms has no alarm features. Which targeted tests are suggested in the ACG guideline?

options.text: Routine colonoscopy for every patient
Celiac serology and fecal calprotectin to assess celiac disease and IBD
Gastric emptying study and HRM
No testing ever

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline suggests celiac serology and fecal calprotectin in patients with IBS and diarrhea symptoms; evaluation remains contextual.

practiceQuestions.stem: In adult chronic idiopathic constipation, which pharmacological recommendation has strong moderate-certainty support in the 2023 joint guideline?

options.text: Polyethylene glycol (PEG)
Magnesium oxide in renal failure
Every patient must undergo manometry first
Immediate colectomy

practiceQuestions.rationale: AGA/ACG recommend PEG for adults with CIC with moderate certainty; this guideline addresses pharmacotherapy, not every constipation phenotype.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with chronic constipation has abnormal simulated evacuation pattern on anorectal manometry. Which statement is best?

options.text: A single pressure pattern always establishes a defecatory disorder
Integrate symptoms and anorectal testing; use complementary evidence and acknowledge limitations
Treat the tracing without clinical context
A normal colonoscopy proves pelvic floor dysfunction

practiceQuestions.rationale: Anorectal test patterns require integrated clinical interpretation; the open review describes test roles and limitations.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which best describes the Johns Hopkins named programme based on its official directory?

options.text: An ACGME-accredited three-year GI fellowship
A one-year programme listed as Non-Standard in the Hopkins directory
An ABIM motility certification course
A non-physician-only research job

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins directory lists the named programme as one year and accrediting body Non-Standard; its department page describes clinical and research training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner asks whether a separate ABIM motility board exam exists. Which answer is supported by current official pages?

options.text: Yes, the ABIM Motility Certification Examination
The named ABIM exam is Gastroenterology; the listed blueprint includes motility domains but no motility-specific exam
ABIM grants board status after any one-year course
Passing this course creates GI eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABIM lists Gastroenterology certification, and its blueprint includes motility disorders (5%); it does not list a separate motility certification exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the 2025 AGA recommendations on refractory gastroparesis interventions?

options.text: Routine G-POEM and gastric electrical stimulation are strongly recommended for all
AGA suggests against routine use of BTI, G-POEM and GES; surgical pyloric intervention has no recommendation
Every patient should have pyloroplasty
Procedures are never considered

practiceQuestions.rationale: The recommendations are conditional suggestions against routine BTI, G-POEM and GES; the guideline makes no recommendation on surgical pyloric procedures.

practiceQuestions.stem: A report of normal gastric emptying is used to tell a fictional patient their symptoms are not real. What is the key educational correction?

options.text: Normal test proves absence of disease
A test result is one piece of evidence; symptoms deserve respectful evaluation and differential reasoning
Repeat every motility test monthly
A DGBI label means symptoms are imagined

practiceQuestions.rationale: Symptoms and objective physiology do not always align, and DGBI is a legitimate clinical framework; use respectful, evidence-calibrated communication.

title: Movement Disorders Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent educational course; not a training programme)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.audience: Neurologists, neurology residents/fellows, and advanced learners; self-study only. This advanced course assumes medical training and supervised neurologic examination experience.
prerequisites.priorTraining: This course is not a route into fellowship. Hopkins lists prior ACGME-accredited neurology residency and ABPN certification/eligibility by start as fellowship admission prerequisites.
prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate educational resource; not accredited training.

objectives: Describe and classify common movement phenomenologies using structured history, examination, and video review while avoiding diagnosis from a single sign.
Apply MDS Parkinson disease criteria as a reasoning framework, recognize red flags and exclusions, and state diagnostic uncertainty appropriately.
Compare major hyperkinetic and hypokinetic syndromes and generate a defensible differential and targeted diagnostic plan.
Interpret non-motor, autonomic, cognitive, sleep, psychiatric, genetic, and medication-related contributions to movement presentations.
Summarize evidence and limitations for symptomatic medication, botulinum toxin, rehabilitation, device-aided treatment, and neuromodulation without providing unsupervised procedural instruction.
Communicate a patient-centred longitudinal management framework, including safety, function, caregiver goals, and multidisciplinary referral.

units.title: Movement phenomenology and examination language
objectives: Distinguish tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, tics, stereotypy, and ataxia by history and examination descriptors.
Separate observed phenomenology from presumed etiology.
topics: Rest, postural, kinetic and task-specific tremor; activation; entrainment and distractibility as clues, not stand-alone diagnoses
Bradykinesia with decrement; tone, gait, balance, ocular motor and coordination exam
Video observation framework, confounds, medications, and documentation
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; neurologic examination; clinical reasoning (course mapping, not a board-issued subtest blueprint)
units.casePractice: Use public MDS Clinical Clues playlist or public Stanford Parkinson's education playlist as links only; compare description-level features, do not download/rehost identifiable media.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page phenomenology matrix for four fictional vignettes; rubric: terminology 40%, differentiating features 30%, uncertainty 20%, respectful language 10%.

units.title: Parkinsonism and Parkinson disease diagnosis
objectives: Define clinical parkinsonism and organize MDS-PD supportive features, red flags, and exclusion criteria.
Differentiate idiopathic PD from drug-induced, vascular, structural, and atypical degenerative parkinsonism using history and exam.
topics: Bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity; disease course and asymmetry
MDS-PD criteria framework; levodopa response and limits; family history and red flags
Role and limits of MRI, dopaminergic imaging and biomarkers; avoid test overinterpretation
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; diagnostic testing; differential diagnosis
units.casePractice: Fictional case conference: distinguish parkinsonism syndrome from cause; label missing evidence and next discriminating question.
units.assessment: Written diagnostic argument with evidence table; rubric: motor syndrome 25%, criteria application 35%, alternatives 25%, uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Parkinson disease treatment decisions and motor complications
objectives: Compare initial dopaminergic treatment choices in context of individual risks and preferences.
Recognize wearing-off, dyskinesia, dose failure, and adverse effects; frame options for specialist review.
topics: AAN 2021 guideline reaffirmed 2025: shared decision discussion of levodopa, dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors
Risk counselling: impulse-control disorder, sleepiness, hallucinations, orthostasis and cognitive vulnerability
Motor fluctuation concepts and advanced-therapy referral decision points; no dosing protocol
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; pharmacology; treatment complications
units.casePractice: Fictional medication-counselling scenario; identify risk factors and questions before treatment choices, not a prescription.
units.assessment: Evidence comparison worksheet; rubric: guideline fidelity 40%, adverse-effect screening 25%, shared decision-making 25%, citations 10%.

units.title: Non-motor Parkinson disease and longitudinal care
objectives: Screen systematically for autonomic, sleep, cognitive, mood, psychosis, pain, and swallowing concerns.
Coordinate longitudinal care with patient goals and appropriate interdisciplinary services.
topics: Constipation, orthostatic symptoms, urinary/sexual symptoms, REM sleep behavior and daytime somnolence
Cognition, depression, anxiety, hallucinations, impulse-control symptoms and caregiver reports
Rehabilitation, speech/swallow evaluation, falls, driving, advance planning and caregiver burden
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; neurobehavior; autonomic; sleep; rehabilitation
units.casePractice: Build a fictional symptom inventory and referral map; use no real patient record.
units.assessment: Care-plan critique; rubric: breadth 30%, prioritization 25%, safety 25%, patient-centredness and team coordination 20%.

units.title: Atypical parkinsonism and rapidly progressive presentations
objectives: Identify clinical clues that should prompt consideration of PSP, MSA, corticobasal syndrome, DLB, vascular or secondary etiologies.
Use longitudinal change, autonomic and ocular motor findings, cognition, and imaging appropriately.
topics: Red flags: early falls, vertical gaze limitation, cerebellar signs, severe autonomic failure, apraxia/cortical signs, early cognitive/psychiatric change
Syndrome-versus-pathology language and diagnostic uncertainty
Avoid claiming single clinical features or imaging are pathognomonic
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; neurodegeneration; clinical localization and differential
units.casePractice: Fictional longitudinal timeline exercise; identify evolving differential and uncertainty, not a definitive pathology label.
units.assessment: Compare two syndrome maps; rubric: discriminating features 40%, limits 25%, safe workup 20%, clear language 15%.

units.title: Tremor syndromes and differential diagnosis
objectives: Classify tremor by activation condition, distribution, frequency context, and associated signs.
Summarize evidence for essential tremor therapies and their evidentiary limits.
topics: Essential tremor phenotype and differential: PD, dystonic, cerebellar, enhanced physiologic, medication/toxic and functional tremor
Medication review and targeted testing; treatment evidence and functional impact
MDS evidence review found propranolol and primidone clinically useful for limb tremor; evidence varies for other interventions and body regions
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; pharmacology; diagnostic reasoning
units.casePractice: Public clinical clue link may support discussion; no video download or diagnostic reuse without permissions.
units.assessment: Tremor comparison table and evidence appraisal; rubric: classification 35%, alternatives 25%, source appraisal 25%, limits 15%.

units.title: Dystonia: phenomenology, causes and treatment principles
objectives: Classify dystonia by body distribution, age of onset, etiology, and temporal/task pattern.
Recognize acquired, genetic and medication-related possibilities and map treatment domains.
topics: Focal, segmental, multifocal, hemidystonia and generalized patterns
Sensory tricks, task specificity, overflow, medication history and age-of-onset reasoning
Botulinum toxin, oral medicines, rehabilitation and DBS as specialist-directed options; no injection or programming instructions
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; neurogenetics; therapeutics
units.casePractice: Compare published public educational examples linked from MDS; do not copy images or assume re-use permission.
units.assessment: Fictional cervical dystonia case: classification and options discussion; rubric: classification 35%, differential 25%, evidence/safety 25%, communication 15%.

units.title: Chorea, Huntington disease and genetic counselling boundaries
objectives: Characterize chorea and distinguish inherited, acquired, medication-related and metabolic differentials.
Explain Huntington disease genetic testing and inheritance only within the proper counselling context.
topics: Motor, cognitive and psychiatric syndrome; differential for chorea
HTT CAG repeat testing and penetrance categories require laboratory interpretation and genetic counselling
Psychiatric, swallowing, nutrition, falls, caregiver and family-system considerations
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; neurogenetics; neuropsychiatry
units.casePractice: Fictional family-history exercise. No predictive testing advice or individual risk determination; refer to genetics professionals.
units.assessment: Differential and counselling-boundary memo; rubric: syndrome 25%, differential 25%, genetic nuance 30%, respectful referral 20%.

units.title: Ataxia and complex gait disorders
objectives: Localize cerebellar, sensory, vestibular, frontal and parkinsonian gait features.
Build a time-course and family-history driven differential, including acquired and genetic causes.
topics: Gait, limb coordination, eye movements, speech and sensory examination
Acute/subacute/chronic time course; medication/toxin, immune, nutritional, structural and genetic causes
When imaging, laboratory testing, or genetics referral changes management
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; cerebellar localization; neurogenetics
units.casePractice: Use NINDS public overview and linked testing resources for fictional phenotype matrix.
units.assessment: Localization and workup map; rubric: localization 35%, timeline 25%, targeted evaluation 25%, uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Myoclonus, tics, stereotypies and paroxysmal movement
objectives: Use phenomenology and temporal pattern to distinguish brief jerks, tic, stereotypy, seizure mimic and episodic movement disorder.
Select the role and limits of EEG, EMG, imaging and medication review.
topics: Positive/negative myoclonus, stimulus sensitivity, suppressibility, premonitory urge and distractibility
Medication/toxic-metabolic and epileptic differentials
When electrodiagnostic studies or video-EEG are appropriate; avoid overdiagnosis from clips
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; epilepsy differential; neurophysiology
units.casePractice: Constructed short vignette set with no actual patient clips; interpret descriptions only.
units.assessment: Phenomenology quiz plus rationale; rubric: terminology 40%, test selection 25%, alternatives 25%, caution 10%.

units.title: Functional movement disorder and ethical communication
objectives: Recognize positive examination features supporting a functional motor diagnosis while maintaining a differential.
Explain a non-stigmatizing, clear, collaborative diagnostic formulation and rehabilitation pathway.
topics: Internal inconsistency/incongruence and positive rule-in findings; no diagnosis solely by exclusion
Coexisting neurologic disease, symptom variability and context
Communication, shared explanation, interdisciplinary rehabilitation, access and stigma
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; behavioral neurology; communication and professionalism
units.casePractice: Use public explanatory materials as linked resources; clinical video gallery reuse rights not assumed.
units.assessment: Write a 150-word fictional explanation; rubric: positive diagnosis 30%, clarity 30%, non-stigmatizing language 25%, next steps/limits 15%.

units.title: Advanced therapies, multidisciplinary practice and evidence synthesis
objectives: Describe referral questions for DBS/device-aided therapy and multidisciplinary selection without treating referral as an indication.
Appraise guideline scope, trial evidence, contraindication uncertainty, and source date.
Integrate a complex fictional case into a defensible educational assessment.
topics: DBS and other advanced therapies: symptoms targeted, expectations, selection and team evaluation
Goal setting, speech/physical/occupational therapy, genetic counselling, neuropsychology and neurosurgical collaboration
Board-blueprint limitations, evidence updating, consent/privacy, and clinical safety
boardDomains: ABPN Neurology: movement disorders; neurotherapeutics; ethics; evidence appraisal
units.casePractice: Final constructed multidisciplinary case conference; no patient chart or image copied.
units.assessment: Integrated oral/written case rubric: localization/phenomenology 20%, differential 20%, evidence 20%, safety/uncertainty 20%, team communication 20%.

assignment.title: Longitudinal movement-disorder reasoning portfolio
deliverables: Phenomenology examination worksheet
Two differential matrices from fictional scenarios
Evidence-and-date appraisal of one current guideline or review
Patient-centred multidisciplinary plan written as a learning exercise
One-page reflection distinguishing course learning from clinical competence
assignment.passStandard: Suggested self-study criterion: at least 80% on each rubric domain after revision; this is not validated, not a board predictor, and not a credential.

assessment.passStandard: No validated pass standard. Suggested review trigger: below 80% on a learning check means revisit sources and seek qualified supervision for clinical questions.
assessment.limitations: Not official ABPN items, not a validated predictor of examination performance, and not a substitute for supervised patient care or institutional assessment.

studyHours.basis: Transparent self-study plan only: 36 hours target video curriculum plus approximately 84 hours readings, case reasoning, assignments, retrieval practice and review. The 36 video hours are not currently met by verified public lecture recordings; this is a plan, not delivered time or clinical training.
studyHours.recommendedPacing: 12 units × approximately 10 total learner hours each; adjust to prior expertise and current source revisions.

mapping.name: The Johns Hopkins Movement Disorders Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page states 2–3 years; eligibility is completion of an ACGME-accredited neurology residency with board-certified or board-eligible status by fellowship start. Describes an intensive first clinical year, individually tailored second year, consult service, and specialty clinics in Parkinson/general movement disorders, neuromodulation/advanced therapies, chemodenervation, ataxia, atypical parkinsonism, Huntington disease, pediatric movement disorders, genetics, and allied therapies. Public schedule PDF is illustrative, not a full didactic syllabus or public inventory of recordings. No ACGME programme accreditation or separate movement-disorders board exam is claimed here.
