unitMap.text: Movement phenomenology and examination language
coveredTopics: Rest, postural, kinetic and task-specific tremor; activation; entrainment and distractibility as clues, not stand-alone diagnoses
Bradykinesia with decrement; tone, gait, balance, ocular motor and coordination exam
Video observation framework, confounds, medications, and documentation

unitMap.text: Parkinsonism and Parkinson disease diagnosis
coveredTopics: Bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity; disease course and asymmetry
MDS-PD criteria framework; levodopa response and limits; family history and red flags
Role and limits of MRI, dopaminergic imaging and biomarkers; avoid test overinterpretation

unitMap.text: Parkinson disease treatment decisions and motor complications
coveredTopics: AAN 2021 guideline reaffirmed 2025: shared decision discussion of levodopa, dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors
Risk counselling: impulse-control disorder, sleepiness, hallucinations, orthostasis and cognitive vulnerability
Motor fluctuation concepts and advanced-therapy referral decision points; no dosing protocol

unitMap.text: Non-motor Parkinson disease and longitudinal care
coveredTopics: Constipation, orthostatic symptoms, urinary/sexual symptoms, REM sleep behavior and daytime somnolence
Cognition, depression, anxiety, hallucinations, impulse-control symptoms and caregiver reports
Rehabilitation, speech/swallow evaluation, falls, driving, advance planning and caregiver burden

unitMap.text: Atypical parkinsonism and rapidly progressive presentations
coveredTopics: Red flags: early falls, vertical gaze limitation, cerebellar signs, severe autonomic failure, apraxia/cortical signs, early cognitive/psychiatric change
Syndrome-versus-pathology language and diagnostic uncertainty
Avoid claiming single clinical features or imaging are pathognomonic

unitMap.text: Tremor syndromes and differential diagnosis
coveredTopics: Essential tremor phenotype and differential: PD, dystonic, cerebellar, enhanced physiologic, medication/toxic and functional tremor
Medication review and targeted testing; treatment evidence and functional impact
MDS evidence review found propranolol and primidone clinically useful for limb tremor; evidence varies for other interventions and body regions

unitMap.text: Dystonia: phenomenology, causes and treatment principles
coveredTopics: Focal, segmental, multifocal, hemidystonia and generalized patterns
Sensory tricks, task specificity, overflow, medication history and age-of-onset reasoning
Botulinum toxin, oral medicines, rehabilitation and DBS as specialist-directed options; no injection or programming instructions

unitMap.text: Chorea, Huntington disease and genetic counselling boundaries
coveredTopics: Motor, cognitive and psychiatric syndrome; differential for chorea
HTT CAG repeat testing and penetrance categories require laboratory interpretation and genetic counselling
Psychiatric, swallowing, nutrition, falls, caregiver and family-system considerations

unitMap.text: Ataxia and complex gait disorders
coveredTopics: Gait, limb coordination, eye movements, speech and sensory examination
Acute/subacute/chronic time course; medication/toxin, immune, nutritional, structural and genetic causes
When imaging, laboratory testing, or genetics referral changes management

unitMap.text: Myoclonus, tics, stereotypies and paroxysmal movement
coveredTopics: Positive/negative myoclonus, stimulus sensitivity, suppressibility, premonitory urge and distractibility
Medication/toxic-metabolic and epileptic differentials
When electrodiagnostic studies or video-EEG are appropriate; avoid overdiagnosis from clips

unitMap.text: Functional movement disorder and ethical communication
coveredTopics: Internal inconsistency/incongruence and positive rule-in findings; no diagnosis solely by exclusion
Coexisting neurologic disease, symptom variability and context
Communication, shared explanation, interdisciplinary rehabilitation, access and stigma

unitMap.text: Advanced therapies, multidisciplinary practice and evidence synthesis
coveredTopics: DBS and other advanced therapies: symptoms targeted, expectations, selection and team evaluation
Goal setting, speech/physical/occupational therapy, genetic counselling, neuropsychology and neurosurgical collaboration
Board-blueprint limitations, evidence updating, consent/privacy, and clinical safety

topicGaps: The independently verified ledger supplies 2.2736 of 36 target hours, leaving a 33.7264-hour external-recording gap. Only atypical parkinsonism and functional movement disorder have a verified long-form recording mapping; units 1, 2, 5, 11 remain only partially covered.

No verified freely accessible, duration-observed recording was added for unit 3 initial PD treatment decisions/motor complications; unit 4 non-motor PD longitudinal care; unit 6 tremor; unit 7 dystonia; unit 8 chorea/Huntington genetics; unit 9 ataxia; unit 10 myoclonus/tics/paroxysmal movements; or unit 12 advanced therapies/DBS multidisciplinary care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional examination shows progressive decrement in amplitude during repetitive finger taps and rigidity. Which statement is the most accurate first reasoning step?

options.text: The motor syndrome supports parkinsonism; cause still requires evaluation.
Parkinson disease is proven by rigidity alone.
A normal blood panel excludes Parkinson disease.
A rest tremor is required in every case.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MDS criteria define parkinsonism as bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity. Establishing syndrome does not by itself establish etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: In the MDS Parkinson disease framework, which feature group must be counterbalanced by additional supportive criteria?

options.text: Supportive criteria
Red flags
Motor symptoms
Family history

practiceQuestions.rationale: Red flags require counterbalancing supportive criteria; supportive criteria increase confidence but do not independently establish diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner claims that a DaT scan distinguishes idiopathic Parkinson disease from multiple system atrophy. Which response best matches NINDS educational guidance?

options.text: DaT imaging can support dopaminergic deficit assessment but cannot distinguish PD from atypical parkinsonism.
It definitively confirms idiopathic PD.
It is a test for Huntington disease.
It replaces the neurologic examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NINDS states DaT imaging can help diagnose PD but cannot distinguish PD from atypical parkinsonism; imaging must be interpreted in context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with early Parkinson disease asks about initial dopaminergic options. What does the AAN guideline advise clinicians to do?

options.text: Counsel about benefits and risks of levodopa, dopamine agonists, and MAO-B inhibitors, tailored to individual characteristics.
Always start a dopamine agonist.
Never discuss levodopa before advanced disease.
Use no treatment until motor symptoms are severe.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2021 AAN guideline, reaffirmed in 2025, recommends counseling on benefits and risks of initial therapy based on individual patient characteristics.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which fictional early-PD patient profile warrants particular caution against dopamine agonist initiation under the AAN guideline?

options.text: A person older than 70 with cognitive impairment and hallucinations
A patient with no known risk factors
A patient asking about guideline evidence
A patient with an isolated ankle sprain

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAN guideline advises against dopamine agonists for patients at higher risk of medication-related adverse effects, including older age, cognitive impairment, hallucinations, sleepiness, or impulse-control disorder history.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has a gradually developing patterned head turn and neck muscle contractions. Which classification dimension is most directly useful before assigning cause?

options.text: Distribution and phenomenology of dystonia
A presumed genetic diagnosis
A single normal MRI
Assuming all dystonia is acquired

practiceQuestions.rationale: Dystonia is classified by distribution and cause; history, exam, and context are needed to evaluate idiopathic, genetic, acquired and other possibilities.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the MDS evidence review of essential tremor treatments?

options.text: Propranolol and primidone were classified clinically useful for limb tremor; evidence for some other body regions/interventions was insufficient.
Every DBS target is proven effective for all tremor types.
The review establishes a universal cure.
Voice tremor evidence was conclusive for all treatments.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The MDS task force review classified propranolol and primidone clinically useful for limb tremor and noted insufficient evidence for voice/head tremor and other interventions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with chorea asks about testing because a parent had Huntington disease. What is the most appropriate educational response?

options.text: Testing decisions require appropriate genetic counselling and specialist discussion; this course cannot provide a personal risk interpretation.
A video alone proves Huntington disease.
Every child is certain to inherit the condition.
Testing has no role in Huntington disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Huntington disease is genetic and HTT repeat testing is used diagnostically, but interpretation, predictive testing and family decisions belong in appropriately counselled clinical care.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the MDS Video Case Library is correct for this independent free course?

options.text: It is member-only; do not count it as free or rehost its cases.
All 1,500+ cases are public domain.
Free-to-view automatically allows copying.
Every case can be downloaded without permission.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MDS explicitly states the case library is for members. Public access to other videos does not grant a license to copy, rehost, or redistribute.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct board-status interpretation of a movement disorders fellowship in this course?

options.text: ABPN lists Neurology certification but no separate Movement Disorders subspecialty examination; fellowship does not independently confer board eligibility.
Completing this course grants board certification.
Every movement disorders fellowship automatically grants an ABPN subspecialty credential.
An AAN directory listing proves ACGME accreditation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Current ABPN examination list identifies neurology and specified subspecialty exams, not Movement Disorders. Programme directory listings are not accreditation determinations, and this course grants no eligibility.

title: Neuro-Ophthalmology Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Advanced self-study for post-clerkship learners, ophthalmology or neurology residents/fellows, and licensed clinicians refreshing knowledge. Not a clinical rotation.
requiredKnowledge: Basic ocular examination, pupils, ocular motility and visual fields
Foundations of neuroimaging and clinical reasoning
Ability to distinguish educational content from patient-specific medical advice
prerequisites.notEquivalentTo: The Hopkins page requires prior residency training for its clinical fellowship; this course does not replace that training or provide supervised patients, examination performance, clinical judgment validation or experience.

objectives: Localize visual dysfunction to afferent, efferent, ocular-motor or supranuclear pathways.
Interpret visual fields, pupils, optic discs, motility findings and OCT as clinical evidence with stated limitations.
Construct safe, source-supported differential diagnoses for optic neuropathy, disc edema, diplopia, pupil abnormalities and neuro-visual syndromes.
Recognize high-risk patterns requiring urgent clinician-led assessment.
Interpret AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG within published diagnostic frameworks and avoid overcalling isolated results.
Use imaging and electrophysiology to answer specific clinical questions rather than as standalone diagnoses.
Appraise date, source type, licensing, uncertainty and patient privacy.
Communicate findings in a concise educational case brief without claiming independent clinical competence.

units.title: Neuro-ophthalmic history, examination and localization
objectives: Construct a focused time-course, laterality, pain, systemic, neurologic, medication and family history.
Perform and document acuity, color/red desaturation, pupils/RAPD, confrontation fields, ocular motility, alignment, eyelids, slit-lamp and fundus elements at a conceptual level.
Localize afferent versus efferent dysfunction and communicate uncertainty and red flags.
topics: The neuro-ophthalmic exam; afferent/efferent pathways; RAPD; color vision; urgent visual loss; examination limitations in a remote or incomplete exam.
boardDomains: AUPO required neuro-ophthalmic examination; patient care; medical knowledge; communication; no separate exam blueprint published.
units.casePractice: Use an invented unilateral visual-loss vignette; state which missing examination elements materially limit localization.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page structured examination and localization note scored for completeness, anatomy and calibrated uncertainty.

units.title: Visual fields and afferent pathway localization
objectives: Describe defect shape, laterality, congruity and reliability before naming a lesion.
Relate monocular, bitemporal and homonymous patterns to retina/nerve, chiasm and retrochiasmal pathways while avoiding over-localization.
Choose when kinetic versus automated perimetry adds information and identify artifacts.
topics: Confrontation versus formal fields; automated static and manual kinetic perimetry; central, arcuate, altitudinal, temporal and homonymous patterns; test reliability; serial change.
boardDomains: AUPO visual-function tests and afferent disorders; clinical interpretation, visual pathway localization.
units.casePractice: Link a pituitary/chiasmal teaching case and map an invented field to the pathway; explain limits of field-based site inference.
units.assessment: Annotated field-localization worksheet with artifact/reliability checklist.

units.title: Optic neuropathy syndrome: tempo, localization and investigation
objectives: Recognize a clinical optic neuropathy pattern using acuity, color, field, pupil and disc findings.
Use tempo and associated features to sort inflammatory, ischemic, compressive, toxic/nutritional, infectious, hereditary, traumatic and infiltrative categories.
Select a differential-driven rather than indiscriminate testing strategy.
topics: Acute versus subacute versus chronic loss; unilateral versus bilateral; pain; dyschromatopsia; OCT and MRI roles; visual-field patterns; mimics and uncertainty.

Public full-length lectures: optic-neuropathy syndrome reasoning; optic neuritis evaluation; ischemic/compressive/infiltrative/infectious causes and optic-disc edema differential (dated treatments require current review).
boardDomains: AUPO afferent pathway disorders and technical examinations; clinical reasoning and practice-based learning.
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional timelines (acute painful monocular; gradual painless bilateral) and list competing mechanisms and discriminating data.
units.assessment: Differential table scored for tempo, localization, test yield and unsafe premature closure.

units.title: Inflammatory and demyelinating optic neuropathy
objectives: Distinguish a typical optic neuritis phenotype from atypical features requiring broader evaluation.
Explain the roles and limitations of MRI, AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG in differential diagnosis.
Apply the international MOGAD framework and NMOSD criteria without treating a single antibody result as a full diagnosis.
topics: MS-associated optic neuritis; AQP4-positive NMOSD; MOGAD; infections, infiltrative mimics; ONTT context; urgency, neuroimmunology collaboration and evolving therapies.

Typical versus atypical optic neuritis; MRI and antibody testing as question-directed adjuncts; distinguish syndrome recognition from diagnosis and avoid using an isolated serology result as a disease label.
boardDomains: AUPO afferent disorders; ACGME clinical neurology; contemporary neuroimmunologic differential.
units.casePractice: Discuss the source-linked Iowa MOGAD educational case, then identify which history, MRI and serology are needed before a label is assigned.
units.assessment: Short-answer diagnostic-criteria map; must name an alternative diagnosis and a test limitation.

units.title: Ischemic, vascular, traumatic and arteritic optic neuropathy
objectives: Compare common clinical features of NAION and arteritic ischemia without assuming a pattern is definitive.
Recognize possible giant cell arteritis as a time-critical systemic emergency and identify the need for urgent clinician-led evaluation.
Place retinal artery occlusion, posterior ischemic and traumatic optic neuropathy in the differential and avoid unsubstantiated treatment claims.
topics: NAION/AAION; GCA symptoms and inflammatory markers; retinal ischemia; posterior ischemic injury; trauma; stroke evaluation; contemporary guideline and local emergency pathways.
Case-based discussion of ischemic optic neuropathy and giant-cell-arteritis red flags; urgent clinician-led evaluation and current guideline/local pathway verification remain essential.
boardDomains: AUPO afferent pathway and systemic disorders; safety, interprofessional coordination.
units.casePractice: For a fictional older adult with transient visual loss and new headache, outline immediate risk questions and parallel referral/workup considerations; do not prescribe.
units.assessment: Urgency-and-safety checklist; full credit requires no delay based on a normal single test.

units.title: Papilledema, raised intracranial pressure and pseudopapilledema
objectives: Distinguish the term papilledema (disc edema from raised ICP) from the wider finding optic-disc edema.
Build a differential for bilateral disc swelling and distinguish it from disc drusen/anatomic elevation using function, fundus, OCT and other imaging as adjuncts.
Explain the need to exclude secondary causes of raised ICP with appropriate neuroimaging/venous assessment and clinician-directed LP sequencing.
topics: True versus pseudo-disc edema; IIH; mass, venous thrombosis, infection, inflammation and hypertension; acuity/fields/OCT; MRI and MRV; LP after appropriate exclusion of contraindications.
Case-based papilledema/IIH and pseudopapilledema coverage; structural disc findings must be interpreted with function and appropriate work-up, not as a standalone diagnosis.
boardDomains: AUPO afferent disorders, testing and systemic implications; safety; patient care.
units.casePractice: Use the linked Iowa IIH teaching case to distinguish a resource case from a generalizable diagnostic rule; no copying clinical images.
units.assessment: Workup-sequence flowchart annotated with unsafe shortcuts and evidence limits.

units.title: Pupils, anisocoria and autonomic pathways
objectives: Characterize anisocoria in bright and dim conditions and assess reactivity, ptosis and ocular motility.
Localize sympathetic versus parasympathetic pathway dysfunction while acknowledging pharmacologic and physiologic mimics.
Recognize painful acute Horner syndrome or pupil-involving third-nerve patterns as requiring urgent clinical assessment.
topics: Pupil light response; RAPD versus anisocoria; Horner syndrome; third-nerve palsy; tonic pupil; pharmacologic testing limitations; carotid/cavernous localization.
boardDomains: AUPO efferent pathway and pupil disorders; examination skills; clinical safety.
units.casePractice: Compare source-linked Horner teaching case and a fictional anisocoria scenario; identify features that alter urgency.
units.assessment: Bright/dim pupil table and localization diagram, rubric: correct pathway, red flags, uncertainty.

units.title: Diplopia, ocular motor palsies and cranial nerve localization
objectives: Determine monocular versus binocular diplopia and document gaze/alignment patterns.
Use associated signs to localize ocular motor nerve, brainstem, cavernous sinus, orbital or neuromuscular-junction syndromes.
Construct a differential for isolated and non-isolated cranial nerve palsies without defaulting to a benign microvascular explanation.
topics: CN III/IV/VI; internuclear ophthalmoplegia; skew; myasthenia; orbital restriction; cavernous sinus; red flags, imaging and follow-up reasoning.
boardDomains: AUPO efferent pathways, ocular motility and systemic disorders; neuroanatomical localization.
units.casePractice: Map a fictional horizontal binocular diplopia and a public EyeRounds INO case to anatomy; do not repeat identifiable records.
units.assessment: Localization grid scored for pattern description, anatomy, red flags and appropriate test rationale.

units.title: Nystagmus, gaze networks and supranuclear eye movements
objectives: Describe nystagmus direction, gaze dependence, fixation effect and associated symptoms.
Differentiate peripheral vestibular clues from central ocular-motor findings without treating any one sign as infallible.
Relate INO, gaze palsy, skew and selected nystagmus patterns to neuroanatomical pathways.
topics: Saccades, pursuit, vestibulo-ocular reflex, gaze holding; nystagmus; INO; skew; dorsal midbrain; cerebellar and brainstem syndromes.
boardDomains: AUPO efferent pathway and supranuclear disorders; clinical neurologic examination.
units.casePractice: Interpret a public INO teaching case using a sign-first description before etiologic hypotheses.
units.assessment: Two-minute oral localization with explicit findings that would change the differential.

units.title: Retro-chiasmal visual syndromes and neuroimaging
objectives: Correlate visual-field complaints with visual pathway anatomy and common brain lesion categories.
State what MRI/CT/orbital/vascular studies can answer and their limitations; match imaging to clinical localization.
Communicate urgent stroke, mass, venous and compressive possibilities without over-interpreting a scan.
topics: Chiasm/pituitary; optic tract, radiations and occipital cortex; stroke; compressive lesion; imaging sequences and contrast/vascular questions; consult coordination.
boardDomains: AUPO frequent neuroimaging requirement and afferent disorders; ACGME clinical neurology; systems practice.
units.casePractice: Use public pituitary-chiasm case as a source-linked exercise; describe field localization and imaging question before viewing the source interpretation.
units.assessment: Imaging request justification: clinical question, modality, urgent differentials, and limitations.

units.title: Systemic, inherited, toxic, infectious and pediatric presentations
objectives: Recognize the broad categories of systemic disorders with neuro-ophthalmic implications.
Use history and phenotype to generate targeted differential diagnoses and tests, not indiscriminate panels.
Identify when age, exposures, family history or systemic symptoms shift urgency or require multidisciplinary care.
topics: Myasthenia and thyroid eye disease; sarcoid/infection/infiltration; toxic/nutritional causes; LHON/inherited disease; pediatric disc anomalies, optic nerve hypoplasia and safeguarding context.
boardDomains: AUPO systemic disorders, afferent and efferent pathway exposure; ethical, culturally respectful care.
units.casePractice: Build a fictional toxic/nutritional/hereditary visual loss differential; use EyeRounds cases for image-linked comparison only on the publisher page.
units.assessment: Structured case memo with focused testing rationale and family/systemic context.

units.title: OCT, electrophysiology, evidence appraisal, communication and scholarship
objectives: Interpret OCT/perimetry as supportive tests while checking quality, segmentation and clinical concordance.
Describe indications/limitations of electrophysiology and longitudinal monitoring.
Appraise source date, evidence type, conflicts, guideline status and licensing; communicate a concise assessment and handoff.
topics: OCT RNFL/GCIPL; visual evoked potentials/ERG; serial monitoring; research questions; documentation; consent/privacy; case conference; interdisciplinary communication.
boardDomains: AUPO technical exams, scholarship and professionalism; six ACGME core competency frame; no specific board blueprint available.
units.casePractice: Submit the integrated source-linked case assignment, acknowledging copyright and limits of image interpretation at a distance.
units.assessment: Culminating written case-and-evidence brief plus 12-question formative quiz; no pass prediction.

assignment.title: Integrated source-linked case conference and evidence brief
assignment.instructions: For a fictional patient vignette of your choice, submit a concise problem representation, afferent/efferent localization, prioritized differential, missing data, justified investigation sequence, urgent risk/escalation discussion, patient-facing explanation, and citations with dates. Use text-only self-created fictional cases or link to a public source case; do not copy patient images, records, or screenshots. State why uncertainty remains and when specialist supervision is required.

rubric.fullCredit: Clear timeline/laterality/function/signs; notes unavailable data and test quality.
Separates syndrome from cause; prioritized alternatives; avoids over-localizing a single test.
Identifies relevant visual/systemic emergencies and explains clinician-led evaluation; no unsafe delay or treatment overreach.
Uses primary/authoritative sources, notes date and evidence type, distinguishes guideline from program rule and acknowledges gaps.
Readable handoff and patient explanation; protects privacy; links to images rather than copying; cites licensed resources.

assignment.passThreshold: 80/100 for this formative course assignment only; not a credential or competence standard.

assessment.format: 12 original formative multiple-choice questions plus integrated case brief
assessment.rubric: Use the assignment rubric; provide rationales for every response and allow revision after feedback.
assessment.limitations: Not official board examination content; not validated against any board; cannot predict passing or establish clinical competence.

unitMap.text: Neuro-ophthalmic history, examination and localization
coveredTopics: The neuro-ophthalmic exam; afferent/efferent pathways; RAPD; color vision; urgent visual loss; examination limitations in a remote or incomplete exam.

unitMap.text: Visual fields and afferent pathway localization
coveredTopics: Confrontation versus formal fields; automated static and manual kinetic perimetry; central, arcuate, altitudinal, temporal and homonymous patterns; test reliability; serial change.

unitMap.text: Optic neuropathy syndrome: tempo, localization and investigation
coveredTopics: Acute versus subacute versus chronic loss; unilateral versus bilateral; pain; dyschromatopsia; OCT and MRI roles; visual-field patterns; mimics and uncertainty.

Public full-length lectures: optic-neuropathy syndrome reasoning; optic neuritis evaluation; ischemic/compressive/infiltrative/infectious causes and optic-disc edema differential (dated treatments require current review).

unitMap.text: Inflammatory and demyelinating optic neuropathy
coveredTopics: MS-associated optic neuritis; AQP4-positive NMOSD; MOGAD; infections, infiltrative mimics; ONTT context; urgency, neuroimmunology collaboration and evolving therapies.

Typical versus atypical optic neuritis; MRI and antibody testing as question-directed adjuncts; distinguish syndrome recognition from diagnosis and avoid using an isolated serology result as a disease label.

unitMap.text: Ischemic, vascular, traumatic and arteritic optic neuropathy
coveredTopics: NAION/AAION; GCA symptoms and inflammatory markers; retinal ischemia; posterior ischemic injury; trauma; stroke evaluation; contemporary guideline and local emergency pathways.
Case-based discussion of ischemic optic neuropathy and giant-cell-arteritis red flags; urgent clinician-led evaluation and current guideline/local pathway verification remain essential.

unitMap.text: Papilledema, raised intracranial pressure and pseudopapilledema
coveredTopics: True versus pseudo-disc edema; IIH; mass, venous thrombosis, infection, inflammation and hypertension; acuity/fields/OCT; MRI and MRV; LP after appropriate exclusion of contraindications.
Case-based papilledema/IIH and pseudopapilledema coverage; structural disc findings must be interpreted with function and appropriate work-up, not as a standalone diagnosis.

unitMap.text: Pupils, anisocoria and autonomic pathways
coveredTopics: Pupil light response; RAPD versus anisocoria; Horner syndrome; third-nerve palsy; tonic pupil; pharmacologic testing limitations; carotid/cavernous localization.

unitMap.text: Diplopia, ocular motor palsies and cranial nerve localization
coveredTopics: CN III/IV/VI; internuclear ophthalmoplegia; skew; myasthenia; orbital restriction; cavernous sinus; red flags, imaging and follow-up reasoning.

unitMap.text: Nystagmus, gaze networks and supranuclear eye movements
coveredTopics: Saccades, pursuit, vestibulo-ocular reflex, gaze holding; nystagmus; INO; skew; dorsal midbrain; cerebellar and brainstem syndromes.

unitMap.text: Retro-chiasmal visual syndromes and neuroimaging
coveredTopics: Chiasm/pituitary; optic tract, radiations and occipital cortex; stroke; compressive lesion; imaging sequences and contrast/vascular questions; consult coordination.

unitMap.text: Systemic, inherited, toxic, infectious and pediatric presentations
coveredTopics: Myasthenia and thyroid eye disease; sarcoid/infection/infiltration; toxic/nutritional causes; LHON/inherited disease; pediatric disc anomalies, optic nerve hypoplasia and safeguarding context.

unitMap.text: OCT, electrophysiology, evidence appraisal, communication and scholarship
coveredTopics: OCT RNFL/GCIPL; visual evoked potentials/ERG; serial monitoring; research questions; documentation; consent/privacy; case conference; interdisciplinary communication.

topicGaps: The observed free public lecture inventory remains far below the 36-hour floor: 2.713056 verified specialty hours and 33.286944 hours residual. Lecture target minutes or authored-script narration are not rendered video and are not counted.

Still not supported by observed recordings at adequate depth: formal perimetry technique/artifact and reliability; full cranial-nerve and supranuclear ocular-motor localization; pediatric presentations; inherited/toxic/nutritional and infectious breadth; electrophysiology; detailed OCT limitations; contemporary treatment evidence and longitudinal monitoring; communication, professionalism, research and ethics.

The three previously listed Moran CORE candidates still have unknown observed durations/playback confirmation and remain uncounted. No separate neuro-ophthalmology board blueprint or Hopkins-specific lecture set/rotation schedule was located. No clinical competence or independent fellowship preparation is claimed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardStatus.separateSpecialtyBoardExam: No separate neuro-ophthalmology board examination/certification was identified in the current UCNS certification list or the official training/career sources checked; neuro-ophthalmology training is a physician subspecialty spanning neurology and ophthalmology, and practitioners hold parent specialty certification in neurology, ophthalmology or both. This is an evidence check, not a definitive legal claim that no future/other credential can exist.
boardStatus.programmeAccreditation: Johns Hopkins listing in the AAN directory says ACGME approval: No; UCNS approval: No; Other approval: Yes and describes AUPO compliance / ACGME-equivalent. This is not ACGME accreditation. AUPO FCC compliance is a separate voluntary fellowship-compliance process.
boardStatus.institutionalVariants: Only the exact Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Wilmer Eye Institute Neuro-Ophthalmology Fellowship in the input packet is represented. This is an actual one-year physician clinical fellowship, not a generic directory category, research-only postdoctoral appointment, or non-physician supplement. The public page does not publish a separate board blueprint.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The Hopkins page states applicants must complete an ACGME-accredited ophthalmology or neurology residency before fellowship and describes an exceptional internationally trained pathway with ECFMG/USMLE conditions; the current program must confirm eligibility directly. AUPO’s published requirements include pathways through listed US and osteopathic parent boards and equivalent international training. This independent self-study course confers no fellowship eligibility, board eligibility, licensure or certification. Check official board and program rules.

sourceCaveats: The Johns Hopkins page shows current public text but no update date; program eligibility and application details should be rechecked with the director.
AAN directory says no ACGME and no UCNS approval, Other approval yes, and describes AUPO compliance / ACGME-equivalent. Do not report ACGME accreditation.

AUPO neuro-ophthalmology requirements PDF is dated 2019-10-14 and is hosted in a 2020 path; verify current requirements directly with AUPO. It gives specialty-wide standards, not audited Hopkins data.

The current UCNS certification page does not list neuro-ophthalmology among its certification exams; absence from a directory is evidence checked, not a promise that no credential can ever be created.

The 2007, 2011, 2013 and 2014 open reviews are foundational and not sole authorities for present-day therapeutic decisions. Contemporary AAO 2025 disc edema review and 2023/2024 neuroimmunology sources were preferred where relevant.
The AAO page is copyrighted; link only. NIH/PMC hosting does not automatically grant redistribution rights; check individual article licenses before reuse.

NOVEL case imagery is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 unless otherwise specified; do not alter/rehost. Moran CORE and EyeRounds content is copyrighted with reuse limits. Case images/patient records have not been copied. Individual case de-identification provenance was not independently audited.

YouTube anti-bot challenges prevented local metadata extraction and direct playback validation. One indexed result showed 33:48 for the exact canonical Moran CORE video ID; three other source pages have unknown runtime and are excluded. Human access check is advisable.

practiceQuestions.stem: Reliable perimetry shows a bitemporal defect respecting the vertical meridian. Which is the best initial localization?

options.text: Optic chiasm
Left optic nerve only
Right occipital cortex only
Bilateral lateral geniculate nuclei

practiceQuestions.rationale: Crossing nasal retinal fibers at the chiasm make a bitemporal pattern a classic localization clue, not proof of cause or precise lesion.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 72-year-old has sudden painless monocular loss, pale disc swelling, new headache and jaw fatigue. What is safest?

options.text: Assume NAION and routine follow-up only.
Urgently evaluate possible giant cell arteritis and communicate visual risk.
Wait for field loss to progress.
Exclude GCA because symptoms are monocular.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Age, acute visual loss and cranial/systemic symptoms raise a time-critical GCA concern. This is recognition and escalation education, not an order set.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 29-year-old develops subacute monocular blur, eye-movement pain, dyschromatopsia and an RAPD. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Establish optic neuropathy phenotype, assess typical/atypical features, and target investigations.
Diagnose MS based on pain alone.
Assume retinal disease without pupil or field exam.
Order every antibody panel as screening.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These findings support afferent dysfunction, not a unique etiology. Exam, field, history and targeted MRI/laboratory investigations inform a broader differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a compatible core neurologic syndrome, appropriate-assay AQP4-IgG positivity and no better alternative. Which best matches NMOSD criteria?

options.text: AQP4-IgG alone diagnoses every patient.
A compatible core clinical characteristic plus AQP4-IgG and exclusion of alternatives supports diagnosis.
Optic neuritis and myelitis are always both required.
OCT replaces MRI and serology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Contemporary criteria permit diagnosis with AQP4-IgG positivity and at least one core clinical characteristic after excluding a better explanation; assay and context matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has low-positive serum MOG-IgG and a compatible event but no supportive clinical/radiologic features identified. Best interpretation?

options.text: Any positive result establishes MOGAD.
Apply the criteria: core event, supporting features for low-positive results, and exclusion of alternatives.
Ignore phenotype and repeat broad testing indefinitely.
AQP4-IgG is irrelevant to differential.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The international framework combines a core demyelinating syndrome, MOG-IgG, additional supporting features when required by the result, and exclusion of alternatives. Test interpretation has assay/timing limitations.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has bilateral disc swelling and headache; secondary raised ICP is unexcluded. Which sequence is safest?

options.text: Label IIH immediately based on demographics.
Characterize optic function, assess secondary causes with appropriate imaging/venous evaluation, then consider LP when clinically appropriate and safe.
Use one OCT value to prove papilledema.
Defer assessment if central acuity is normal.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Papilledema is a finding of raised ICP; secondary causes require assessment. LP sequence is clinician-directed after considering imaging and contraindications. Normal central acuity does not exclude field risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has elevated-appearing discs, preserved function and possible buried drusen. What is most accurate?

options.text: Every elevated disc is papilledema.
Pseudopapilledema is possible; correlate multimodal imaging with function and full clinical assessment.
Normal central acuity excludes papilledema.
A single RNFL number is definitive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Drusen and anatomic variants can mimic edema. Ancillary imaging helps but is not an isolated etiologic diagnosis and cannot dismiss raised ICP by itself.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with acute painful unilateral ptosis has mild miosis more apparent in darkness. Highest-priority interpretation?

options.text: Possible acute Horner syndrome; localize and urgently evaluate dangerous causes such as carotid pathology.
Physiologic anisocoria is proven.
Classic isolated afferent defect.
No further assessment is ever needed if the pupil reacts.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Miosis/ptosis more apparent in darkness suggests sympathetic pathway dysfunction. Acute pain warrants urgent assessment; the sign alone does not prove cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with new binocular diplopia has ptosis, impaired adduction/elevation and new pupil enlargement. What is safest?

options.text: Assume a benign chronic microvascular palsy.
Recognize a possible third-nerve pattern and arrange urgent clinician-led evaluation for compressive/vascular causes.
Localize to the chiasm.
Normal acuity rules out cranial neuropathy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This may localize to the oculomotor pathway; an acute pupil-involving pattern may signal a compressive/vascular emergency. Full evaluation and imaging decisions are contextual.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with horizontal binocular diplopia cannot abduct one eye. Best first principle?

options.text: Describe alignment, confirm binocular diplopia, examine associated signs and localize along the sixth-nerve course before narrowing cause.
A sixth-nerve palsy always means raised ICP.
The nerve has a short course, so associated signs are unhelpful.
Neuroimaging is never relevant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The sixth nerve has a long course and associated signs aid localization. Causes vary; descriptive examination precedes etiologic certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: OCT shows thick peripapillary RNFL in suspected disc edema. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: OCT alone proves papilledema caused by IIH.
Check image quality/segmentation and correlate with function, fundus, history and broader workup.
OCT is irrelevant.
A normal macular scan excludes optic neuropathy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: OCT aids assessment and follow-up but quality, segmentation, structural variants and clinical context matter; it cannot independently establish etiology.

practiceQuestions.stem: A single field appears homonymous, but reliability indices are poor and the fictional learner had trouble understanding instructions. Best action?

options.text: Report a definitive occipital lesion.
Acknowledge reliability limits, repeat/choose an appropriate test and integrate examination/imaging.
Ignore reliability indices.
Assume intentional symptoms.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Poor test reliability prevents confident localization or inferences about intent; repeat or adapt testing and integrate other evidence.

title: Neurocritical Care Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced learner: physicians or trainees who already have substantial neurology/neurosurgery/critical-care foundations; this independent course is not an admissions or board-eligibility pathway.

Recommended prior study: neuroanatomy/neurophysiology; neurologic examination and localization; basic CT/MRI/vascular imaging; pharmacology; respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, infectious disease, and general ICU physiology; evidence appraisal and biostatistics.
Before using any clinical content, consult current local protocols, supervising clinicians and current specialty guidance; hands-on skill requires supervised accredited clinical training.
objectives: Synthesize neurologic examination, neuroanatomy, physiology, imaging, EEG and monitoring into a prioritized differential without over-reading single measurements.

Apply contemporary guideline-based reasoning to acute ischemic stroke, intracerebral/subarachnoid hemorrhage, TBI, seizures/status, infections and postoperative neurosurgical complications while identifying evidence limits and emergencies requiring escalation.

Reason through multisystem critical illness, including ventilation, hemodynamics, renal/electrolyte/endocrine, infection, hematology, temperature, nutrition and prophylaxis in the context of brain injury.
Explain indications, interpretation limits, complications and safety checks for common diagnostic monitoring and procedures; this course does not confer procedural competence.
Distinguish prognostication from determination of death by neurologic criteria and communicate uncertainty, family-centered goals, ethics and end-of-life decisions.
Critically appraise research and guidelines, document uncertainty and recognize when recommendations are date-sensitive.

units.title: Neuro-ICU approach, examination and physiology
objectives: Construct a systematic approach to coma and acute neurologic deterioration.
Relate cerebral blood flow, autoregulation, intracranial compliance, CSF and oxygen delivery to bedside findings.
Identify confounders from sedation, temperature, metabolism and systemic illness.
topics: Localization and structured neurologic examination in the ICU; coma/delirium; Glasgow Coma Scale and FOUR score limits; Monro-Kellie doctrine; cerebral perfusion and autoregulation; neuropharmacology; safety-first stabilization
units.casePractice: Fictional oral localization exercise with medication, temperature and metabolic confounders; no real-patient record.
units.assessment: Create a prioritized coma differential and 10-minute handoff; rubric: examination/localization (30%), reversible mimics (30%), physiologic reasoning (25%), uncertainty/communication (15%).

units.title: Airway, ventilation, hemodynamics and shock
objectives: Integrate brain-protective ventilation with oxygenation, CO2 and hemodynamic goals.
Differentiate common shock phenotypes and evaluate multimodal hemodynamic data.
Recognize cardiopulmonary complications of LVAD/ECMO and when subspecialty help is required.
topics: Airway and tracheostomy principles; invasive/noninvasive ventilation; ARDS; pulmonary edema/aspiration; shock, vasopressors and inotropes; arterial waveform, echo, POCUS; arrhythmia, ACS, ECMO/LVAD neurologic complications
units.casePractice: Fictional case of worsening oxygenation and neurologic exam during shock; learners chart competing causes and escalation triggers.
units.assessment: Ventilator/hemodynamic interpretation worksheet, graded for data integration (40%), safety and differential (30%), justified next tests/escalation (20%), clarity (10%).

units.title: Neuroimaging, CSF and multimodality monitoring
objectives: Choose and interpret the role/limits of CT, MRI, CTA/CTV, perfusion and angiography in acute brain injury.
Compare EEG, ICP/EVD, TCD, brain tissue oxygen and multimodality monitoring signals.
Identify artifact, sampling, procedural and interpretation limitations.
topics: Noncontrast CT and MRI sequences; vascular imaging; EEG/cEEG/qEEG; CSF studies; ICP/EVD indications and complications; TCD; PbtO2 and multimodal monitoring; bedside ultrasound; EMG basics
units.casePractice: Use linked de-identified published images only in situ; compare a learner's written read with the source's original discussion; never download/rehost images.
units.assessment: Two modality-selection vignettes; rubric: indication (25%), interpretation (35%), limitations/artifact (25%), safe escalation (15%).

units.title: Intracranial hypertension, edema and herniation
objectives: Recognize deteriorating intracranial compliance and physiologic emergencies.
Compare disease-specific approaches to osmotherapy and other ICP therapies without assuming outcome benefit.
Analyze monitoring and treatment risk, complications and evidence certainty.
topics: ICP waveforms/CPP; edema mechanisms; hyperosmolar therapy; CSF diversion; ventilation and temperature; positioning; decompression; monitoring/safety; syndrome-specific evidence
units.casePractice: Fictional serial neurologic examination/ICP trend case; learners must separate trend, measurement validity, cause and response.
units.assessment: Evidence grid for a single ICP intervention; scored for disease-specific evidence (35%), safety/monitoring (30%), limits (20%), readable synthesis (15%).

units.title: Acute ischemic stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis
objectives: Assess acute ischemic stroke for reperfusion and identify relevant contraindication/eligibility uncertainty.
Recognize malignant infarction, edema, posterior circulation and venous thrombosis threats.
Integrate stroke-team, neurocritical and neurointerventional roles.
topics: Stroke systems and imaging; thrombolysis/thrombectomy selection as date-sensitive; large hemispheric and basilar infarction; cerebral edema; antithrombotics; CVST; stroke in pregnancy
units.casePractice: Fictional acute stroke triage case with unknown last-known-well and incomplete imaging: state missing data before proposing a pathway.
units.assessment: Decision memo graded for time-critical workflow (25%), guideline qualification (35%), differential/risk (25%), communication (15%).

units.title: Intracerebral hemorrhage, SAH and vascular emergencies
objectives: Differentiate hemorrhage patterns and complications requiring urgent multidisciplinary management.
Explain current guideline roles in reversal, BP, seizure prophylaxis, hydrocephalus and neuroprognostication.
Avoid premature outcome prediction and identify guideline update dates.
topics: ICH, cerebellar/intraventricular hemorrhage; antithrombotic-associated ICH; aneurysmal/nonaneurysmal SAH; vasospasm/delayed cerebral ischemia; aneurysm/AVM/cavernoma; reversal agents; hydrocephalus/EVD complications
units.casePractice: Fictional CT report and hemodynamic vignette; link to authentic de-identified resource in place, subject to its terms.
units.assessment: Comparative care-pathway map scored for diagnosis/complication (30%), current source use (35%), uncertainty/safety (20%), teamwork (15%).

units.title: Traumatic brain and spinal cord injury
objectives: Reason through secondary brain injury prevention in TBI and severe spinal injury.
Interpret ICP and imaging in context of injury, systemic trauma and serial change.
Communicate uncertainty in neuroprognostication and prevent self-fulfilling prediction.
topics: TBI patterns; contusion, EDH/SDH, DAI; polytrauma; cervical spine and neurogenic shock; ICP and edema; seizure prophylaxis as evidence-specific; DVT prevention; neuroprognostication; spinal cord injury
units.casePractice: Fictional polytrauma timeline; learners identify confounders and distinguish physiologic management from long-term prediction.
units.assessment: Structured oral case, scored for primary/secondary injury (30%), systems integration (25%), evidence/uncertainty (25%), communication (20%).

units.title: Seizures, status epilepticus and ICU EEG
objectives: Recognize convulsive and nonconvulsive status and construct a stabilization/evaluation sequence.
Interpret EEG concepts and distinguish periodic/rhythmic patterns from clinical seizure labels.
Assess antiseizure therapy choices, adverse effects and evidence limitations.
topics: Convulsive/refractory status; cEEG; seizure mimics; post-arrest EEG; prophylaxis contexts; antiseizure medication interactions; EEG artifact; neuroprognostication
units.casePractice: Fictional post-convulsive persistent unresponsiveness with a described EEG pattern; use EEG interpretation cautiously and no copied tracings.
units.assessment: EEG reasoning exercise scored for clinical state (25%), pattern/context (35%), safe management rationale (25%), limits (15%).

units.title: Coma, cardiac arrest, neuroprognostication and brain death
objectives: Separate coma differential, prognostication and death determination as distinct tasks.
Apply 2023 multisociety BD/DNC prerequisites and ancillary testing indications at a conceptual level; refer to local policy and qualified clinicians.
Communicate uncertainty, timelines, goals and organ donation considerations ethically.
topics: Coma; post-arrest care and multimodal prognosis; medication/temperature confounding; BD/DNC known catastrophic injury, prerequisites, examination, apnea testing, ancillary studies; family communication and donation
boardDomains: 05.A-I ethics, prognostication, end-of-life and donor care
units.casePractice: Fictional post-arrest scenario explicitly not a real BD/DNC determination; learners list prerequisites and reasons to defer.
units.assessment: Communication role-play with checklist: prerequisites (35%), prognosis vs determination (25%), guideline adherence (25%), respectful language (15%).

units.title: Infections, neuromuscular emergencies and special populations
objectives: Build a prioritized differential for acute CNS infection and systemic infection with brain dysfunction.
Recognize respiratory/autonomic failure in neuromuscular crises and medication complications.
Adapt reasoning for pregnancy, transplant, cancer and pediatric patients while acknowledging limited track scope.
topics: Meningitis/encephalitis/ventriculitis/abscess; sepsis; GBS/myasthenic crisis/rhabdomyolysis; autoimmune encephalitis; neuro-oncology/immune therapy; pregnancy/eclampsia/PRES/RCVS; transplant; pediatric considerations
units.casePractice: Fictional differential matrix for altered mental status in an immunosuppressed patient; use open published cases only under original site terms.
units.assessment: Differential and escalation memo, rubric: coverage/priority (35%), testing rationale (30%), special-population safety (20%), evidence/source currency (15%).

units.title: Renal, endocrine, hematologic, GI and general ICU care
objectives: Integrate multiorgan dysfunction, acid-base and electrolyte data into neurologic assessment.
Recognize neuroendocrine syndromes and effects of organ failure on drug clearance.
Apply general ICU prevention, nutrition, temperature, transfusion and thrombosis reasoning without replacing local protocols.
topics: AKI/RRT; sodium/water disorders, DI/SIADH/cerebral salt wasting; glucose, thyroid/adrenal/pituitary; coagulopathy/DIC/transfusion/VTE; liver failure, abdominal emergencies; nutrition, temperature, delirium, mobility, VAP/CAUTI/ulcer prevention
units.casePractice: Fictional laboratory trend case; identify whether an abnormality could confound examination or drug clearance, then name evidence needed.
units.assessment: Multisystem diagnostic synthesis rubric: physiology (30%), medication/monitoring (25%), neurologic implication (25%), prioritized plan and uncertainty (20%).

units.title: Neurosurgery, safety, evidence appraisal and professional practice
objectives: Recognize postoperative hemorrhage, ischemia, infection, CSF leak, seizures and EVD complications.
Evaluate study design, guideline grading, external validity and changing standards.
Lead family-centered discussion, conflict resolution, shared decisions, quality and safety learning.
topics: Neurosurgical/perioperative emergencies; drain/device complications; research methods/journal club; safety/quality; ethics, capacity/decision makers, DNR, palliative care, withdrawal/withholding, donation; team leadership
units.casePractice: Fictional post-operative deterioration and family conference exercise; separate medical uncertainty from values and consent.
units.assessment: Journal-club plus family conference; rubric: critical appraisal (35%), safety/complication recognition (25%), ethics/communication (25%), actionable reflective learning (15%).

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) Neurocritical Care subspecialty certification (co-sponsored with ABA, ABEM, ABIM, ABNS)
United Council for Neurologic Subspecialties (UCNS) Neurocritical Care certification (separate credentialing pathway)
medical.boardStatus: A distinct physician subspecialty certificate in Neurocritical Care exists: ABPN has administered the ABMS-approved subspecialty examination since 2021. UCNS has independently offered an NCC certification examination since 2007 and states it continues. These are different credentials; UCNS certification does not transfer to ABPN certification. They are not a single primary-specialty board exam. The ABPN page checked 2026-10-07 lists the Oct 5–9, 2026 examination (currently in progress on the check date), its application deadlines as passed, and 2028 as the next choice of dates. ABPN lists post-practice-pathway training requirements after the 2021–2026 practice pathway; candidates must verify the relevant sponsoring primary board's rules. The program's ACGME accreditation and UCNS accreditation do not confer certification or candidate eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course neither establishes nor evaluates board eligibility. ABPN eligibility depends on primary-board certification and the candidate's training pathway and sponsoring-board rules; UCNS has separate requirements. ABPN's transitional practice pathway is described for examination administrations 2021–2026; do not assume it applies to a later exam. Confirm current details directly with ABPN/one's primary board and UCNS. Johns Hopkins program admission prerequisites are not board exam eligibility.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: The Johns Hopkins Fellowship in Neurocritical Care
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The public program page states ACGME accreditation since July 2022 and continuing UCNS accreditation; two years of training; eligible residency/fellowship backgrounds including neurology, neurosurgery, internal medicine, emergency medicine and anesthesiology/critical care medicine. Clinical page describes JHH and Johns Hopkins Bayview neurocritical care, MICU, surgical trauma/burns ICU, CICU, airway and electives (EEG, TCD, stroke, pharmacology, simulation/research); elective time is described as about 10 months in longitudinal two-week blocks. Education page describes bootcamp, weekly protected didactics, EEG rounds, simulation, board review and monthly sessions. Exact full institutional lecture recordings and complete case volumes are not publicly itemized. This is the exact Johns Hopkins variant in the supplied packet; no additional institution is conflated. The page does not advertise a distinct pediatric NCC track.

officialProgrammes.name: Neurocritical care Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This is the single Johns Hopkins clinical physician fellowship from the exact MED-094 packet. Neurocritical Care is an actual clinical physician subspecialty, not a research-only or generic directory label. The Johns Hopkins page reports both ACGME and UCNS accreditation. ABPN certification (ABMS-approved) and UCNS certification are distinct exam/credentialing routes; the UCNS route is not ABMS board certification. ACGME requirements define two entry formats (NCC-1 and NCC-2) and adult physiologic/procedural competencies; they are not a transcript of the Johns Hopkins rotation schedule. No research-only, non-physician, combined, pediatric-specific, or additional institutional variants are asserted.
sourceCaveats: Johns Hopkins official public pages identify a clinical fellowship, accreditation, broad eligibility and selected rotations/didactics, but do not publish a complete didactic recording corpus, all case volumes, or the time spent in each activity.
The ABPN detailed content blueprint was posted December 23, 2021, so it is an exam-domain mapping rather than a guarantee of current question weights; check the board's current page.

The ABPN public page checked Oct 7, 2026 shows exam days Oct 5–9, 2026 and says next choice of dates 2028; 2026 application deadlines had passed. Board policies can change; individual primary boards may set additional requirements.

Videos counted only when a public page/metadata revealed a full runtime and page was publicly viewable; no playlist count is extrapolated, no inaccessible video is counted, and no planned recording is counted. Runtime evidence method is recorded in the separate ledger.

MedPix showed a government funding lapse notice and current cases/rights could not be inspected. The separately cited PMC paper is authentic clinical imaging but rehosting is not licensed by free viewing.

Clinical material is educational and date-sensitive. Human clinical review is not performed. No affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence or certification is provided or implied.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional post-arrest patient is comatose with absent brainstem reflexes. The cause of injury is not established, recent sedatives may remain active, and severe metabolic abnormalities are present. Which is the best next educational conclusion?

options.text: Proceed directly to BD/DNC determination because the examination is absent.
Obtain an ancillary cerebral perfusion test now to bypass confounders.
Do not initiate BD/DNC evaluation until catastrophic permanent injury and required prerequisites are established and confounders addressed.
Use a single EEG as a substitute for the clinical evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2023 multisociety guideline requires an identified catastrophic, permanent brain injury before initiating evaluation and treats hypothermia/high sedating medication and other confounders as reasons not to use ancillary testing to bypass prerequisites. This fictional case does not support determination.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner summarizes the 2020 NCS cerebral edema guideline as proving that hyperosmolar therapy improves long-term neurologic outcome in every neurocritical care diagnosis. What is the best correction?

options.text: Correct; lowering ICP is a validated surrogate for improved neurologic outcome in all diseases.
The guideline found possible reduction in ICP/edema in several conditions, but neurologic outcome benefit was not established; treatment choice and monitoring remain disease- and safety-specific.
The guideline recommends corticosteroids for all cerebral edema.
The guideline shows mannitol and hypertonic saline are clinically interchangeable in all cases.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline reports potential reduction in ICP/edema but no apparent neurologic outcome effect, stresses low-quality evidence and safety monitoring, and finds disease-specific differences; corticosteroid findings differ by underlying condition.

practiceQuestions.stem: A deeply sedated patient has a new asymmetric pupil and worsening responsiveness. Which response best reflects neurocritical-care reasoning?

options.text: Assume medication effect because the patient is sedated.
Reassess urgently, verify examination/physiology and medication context, consider a new structural or vascular emergency, and communicate/escalate through the treating team.
Wait until sedation is stopped at the next routine review.
Use a prognostic score to exclude structural injury.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A focal change can signal acute deterioration; sedation is a confounder but cannot safely explain away new asymmetry. This is a general educational reasoning question, not a patient-specific order.

practiceQuestions.stem: For an unresponsive neuro-ICU patient, what best characterizes the choice of EEG, CT/MRI, vascular imaging and CSF studies?

options.text: Order the same complete battery for every patient.
Select tests to address a prioritized differential and specific clinical question; interpret technical and temporal limits.
An EEG replaces structural imaging when coma is unexplained.
A normal initial CT excludes all acute neurologic pathology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPN blueprint enumerates diagnostic modalities, but selection depends on context, and each modality has limits. A single normal test does not exclude all mechanisms.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which distinction between ACGME training formats is correct in the 2025 reformatted requirements?

options.text: NCC-1 is 12 months after neurology residency; NCC-2 is 24 months after surgery.
NCC-1 is 24 months after specified residency training; NCC-2 is 12 months after specified critical-care fellowship or neurosurgery pathway.
Both formats are 24 months and only open to neurologists.
ACGME requirements are identical to ABPN board exam eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME describes NCC-1 as 24 months after listed residency programs and NCC-2 as 12 months after certain critical-care fellowships or completion/matriculation in neurological surgery residency. Program requirements and board eligibility are different documents.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee reports that UCNS NCC certification automatically transfers to ABPN NCC certification because ABPN is ABMS-approved. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Correct; UCNS and ABPN certificates are identical.
UCNS says its certification does not transfer to the newly created ABPN subspecialty certification; each route has its own process.
Neither board offers an NCC examination.
Only ACGME program accreditation can issue either physician certificate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: UCNS FAQ explicitly states UCNS certification does not transfer to the ABPN subspecialty certification; it continues its own certification examination. Accreditation and certification are separate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A study reports that an intervention lowers ICP in a small cohort. Which appraisal is most appropriate before claiming it improves outcomes?

options.text: Assume that any ICP reduction causes better functional recovery.
Examine study design, population, endpoint, confounding, harms and certainty; a physiologic endpoint does not establish patient-centered outcome benefit.
Ignore adverse effects because ICP is a surrogate.
Apply the finding to every etiology of cerebral edema.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NCS edema guideline discusses limited evidence and lack of demonstrated neurologic outcome effects for hyperosmolar therapies; evidence should be applied within population and endpoint limits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with acute neurologic injury also has renal failure, temperature abnormality and recent sedative exposure. Why does this matter when interpreting the examination?

options.text: These features can affect physiology, drug clearance and the neurologic examination; they belong in the confounder assessment.
They are irrelevant to neurologic assessment.
Renal failure proves permanent neurologic injury.
An abnormal examination under sedation is always definitive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The board blueprint includes renal physiology and neuropharmacology; 2023 BD/DNC guidance highlights medication and temperature confounders. This is not a specific medication washout prescription.

practiceQuestions.stem: A family asks whether lack of awakening today means the patient will never recover. What is the best communication approach?

options.text: Give a definitive prognosis based on the current examination alone.
Separate what is known from uncertain, explain timing/confounders and planned reassessment, and avoid promises or premature certainty.
Avoid all communication until a final outcome is known.
Use BD/DNC terminology to simplify the conversation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ethical practice and neuroprognostication require clear uncertainty, family-centered communication and separation of prognosis from BD/DNC determination; a single early finding is insufficient.

practiceQuestions.stem: A reviewer uses a 2019 coma/brain-death video as the sole authority for present-day BD/DNC practice. Which curriculum response is best?

options.text: Accept it because educational videos do not need dates.
Keep it as historical context only, then read the current 2023 multisociety guideline and applicable local/jurisdictional policy.
Replace the guideline with social media comments.
Use a planned course recording as if already published.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The video is dated and contains historical commentary; the 2023 guideline is the current authoritative clinical reference identified here. Planned original media are not available evidence or counted hours.

topicGaps: Observed free specialty-video ledger is 13.454167 h of the 36.0-h target; actual remaining gap is 22.545833 h. Scripted material is not rendered video and contributes zero hours.

Public teaching coverage remains uneven: the 2024-revised McDonald criteria and full criteria paper need direct primary-source study; MS DMT selection/safety, vaccination and reproductive planning are not comprehensively covered by the newly added recordings.

MOGAD/NMOSD treatment and longitudinal care, adult and child pathway distinctions, and rare neuroinfectious disease breadth remain dependent on current primary guidelines, clinical supervision and specialist teaching beyond the linked public talks.

Public recording hours cannot substitute for clinical rotations, supervised practice, cases, or institutional fellow conferences; Hopkins publishes no public hour-by-hour curriculum or complete recording archive.

Source items with unobserved direct runtime/access remain uncounted: Stanford embedded collections; NIH VideoCast runtime; Hopkins fellow recordings; Global Health and Neuroimmunology lecture duration; NMOSD pathogenesis, vision-health, relapse-adjudication, special-populations and tolerization videos whose runtimes were visible only on other watch-page recommendation lists; and contact-to-view encephalitis webinars.

Six original scripts were required/planned to address priority gaps; this first expansion authors four complete episodes. Remaining hour gap cannot responsibly be filled with targets, readings, trailers, duplicated series, or fabricated lecture lengths.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital physician fellowship, with track variants preserved exactly as listed on the official current page. The broad title is an actual institutional physician fellowship, but combines clinical specialty education and investigator development. It is not an ABPN/ABMS specialty or subspecialty certificate. The directory label is a generic institutional accreditation-category field (“Non-Standard”), not a fellowship-specific board exam. The research track is a physician clinical/research combination, not research-only/non-physician training. No Harvard-affiliated second program variant was identified in the assigned packet.
sourceCaveats: Johns Hopkins identifies the fellowship as Non-Standard in its directory. This is not evidence of ACGME accreditation; no affiliation/accreditation is claimed.
Hopkins official page states eligibility, named tracks and intermittent focused infection offering; there is no public detailed didactic hour ledger.

ABPN/ABMS directories list no Neuroimmunology or Neuroinfectious Disease board examination/certificate. Absence from directory checked on 2026-10-07 should not be misconstrued as permanent; recheck official boards.
AAN consensus curriculum is a recommended educational framework, not an ABPN exam blueprint or Hopkins-specific curriculum.
IDSA encephalitis guidance is archived (2008); current practice must use current sources and local expert guidance. NIH HIV OI guidance is living and date-sensitive.

Video hours count only six unique specialty video IDs with publicly observed durations and public viewing evidence; one candidate lecture with embedded-only runtime, short clips, unknown-length archives and planned original material are excluded.
No images, slides, patient records or transcripts were copied. Rights to linked third-party media remain with their owners.
No claims about clinical case volume, supervised procedural skill, guaranteed passing, individual eligibility or patient-specific treatment are made.

Human clinical review is NOT PERFORMED. Independent education does not provide institutional affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, competence, certification or care authorization.

topicGaps: Observed free specialty-video ledger is 13.454167 h of the 36.0-h target; actual remaining gap is 22.545833 h. Scripted material is not rendered video and contributes zero hours.

Public teaching coverage remains uneven: the 2024-revised McDonald criteria and full criteria paper need direct primary-source study; MS DMT selection/safety, vaccination and reproductive planning are not comprehensively covered by the newly added recordings.

MOGAD/NMOSD treatment and longitudinal care, adult and child pathway distinctions, and rare neuroinfectious disease breadth remain dependent on current primary guidelines, clinical supervision and specialist teaching beyond the linked public talks.

Public recording hours cannot substitute for clinical rotations, supervised practice, cases, or institutional fellow conferences; Hopkins publishes no public hour-by-hour curriculum or complete recording archive.

Source items with unobserved direct runtime/access remain uncounted: Stanford embedded collections; NIH VideoCast runtime; Hopkins fellow recordings; Global Health and Neuroimmunology lecture duration; NMOSD pathogenesis, vision-health, relapse-adjudication, special-populations and tolerization videos whose runtimes were visible only on other watch-page recommendation lists; and contact-to-view encephalitis webinars.

Six original scripts were required/planned to address priority gaps; this first expansion authors four complete episodes. Remaining hour gap cannot responsibly be filled with targets, readings, trailers, duplicated series, or fabricated lecture lengths.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked what is required to diagnose MOGAD under the international proposed framework. Which is the best response?

options.text: Any serum MOG-IgG positivity is sufficient.
A compatible core demyelinating event, MOG-IgG evidence interpreted with assay/result strength, and exclusion of better alternatives.
AQP4-IgG positivity plus optic neuritis.
A single nonspecific MRI lesion and a low-positive antibody.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The proposed criteria use a compatible core event, MOG-IgG, and exclusion of alternative diagnoses; low-positive results need supporting clinical/radiologic features. A positive antibody alone is not the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a new inflammatory optic neuritis has a low-positive serum MOG-IgG. Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Label MOGAD immediately because specificity is absolute.
Ignore clinical phenotype and repeat broad panels.
Review assay type/timing and phenotype, look for required supporting features and exclude MS/AQP4-NMOSD or other explanations.
Use low-positive MOG-IgG as proof of MS.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The criteria caution against interpreting low-positive results without supportive phenotype/features and exclusion of competing diagnoses; test timing and method matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician evaluates subacute memory loss, new seizures and behavioral change. Which is the best general diagnostic principle?

options.text: A positive neuronal antibody panel alone establishes autoimmune encephalitis.
Work in parallel on the syndrome, infectious and other mimics, MRI/EEG/CSF findings, and antibody results matched to phenotype.
A normal MRI excludes autoimmune encephalitis.
Infection need not be considered when autoimmune disease is possible.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Syndrome-based assessment and active exclusion of infection and other mimics reduce misdiagnosis; isolated tests do not replace clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: An immunocompromised patient has a compatible meningitis syndrome but a negative multiplex CSF panel. What is the safest inference?

options.text: All infectious etiologies are excluded.
The panel result must be interpreted against its organism coverage and test performance; targeted testing may still be needed.
Autoimmune encephalitis is proven.
No further testing is useful.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Multiplex panels cover a defined set and have organism-specific limitations. A negative panel cannot exclude pathogens not included or those for which sensitivity is inadequate; consult current microbiology guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which resource is the current living U.S. guideline portal for adult/adolescent HIV opportunistic infections, including CNS chapters?

options.text: Archived IDSA encephalitis guideline alone.
NIH ClinicalInfo Adult and Adolescent Opportunistic Infection guideline portal.
A video playlist.
An institutional fellowship directory.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIH ClinicalInfo maintains the living HIV OI guidelines with CNS-relevant chapters; the portal reported updates through May 27, 2026 on date checked.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient develops a focal spinal cord syndrome. Which first principle best protects against a premature immune diagnosis?

options.text: Assume inflammatory myelitis when symptoms are subacute.
Localize the syndrome and urgently evaluate compressive and other dangerous mimics while building an exposure- and phenotype-informed differential.
Order every antibody available before imaging.
Treat the MRI as diagnostic without clinical context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Myelopathy has urgent compressive, vascular, infectious, neoplastic, metabolic and inflammatory causes. Safe sequencing and syndrome localization precede premature labeling.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes institutional training from board certification in this fellowship?

options.text: Completion grants a dedicated ABPN Neuroimmunology board certificate.
Johns Hopkins lists the fellowship as non-standard; ABPN lists no separate Neuroimmunology/Neuroinfectious Disease subspecialty exam.
The program is an ACGME residency because it is in a directory.
A fellowship page determines board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins’s directory identifies an accrediting body classification of “Non-Standard”; ABPN’s listed exams contain no dedicated neuroimmunology/neuroinfectious certificate. Primary neurology certification has separate requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: The Hopkins fellowship page describes an occasional focused neurological-infections fellowship. Which is the most accurate interpretation?

options.text: It is a distinct, annually available, ACGME-accredited board fellowship.
The focused infections offering is not offered every year; the broader named program includes distinct clinical/research and myelitis tracks.
It is a non-physician generic infection course.
It is an ABIM Infectious Disease residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official Hopkins page says a focused fellowship of neurological infections is not offered every year. The page separately names Neuroimmunology/MS Clinical, Combined Clinical and Research, and Myelitis/Myelopathies tracks.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is considering the 2008 IDSA encephalitis guideline as a current treatment protocol. What should they note?

options.text: IDSA marks it archived; use it as historical framework only and verify current guidance and local protocols.
It has no date and is automatically current.
Its publication means all treatment recommendations are unchanged.
It replaces infectious diseases consultation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The IDSA page labels the 2008 guideline archived. The curriculum flags its age and requires current cross-checking rather than treating it as current protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with HIV and progressive cognitive/motor symptoms has a negative routine CSF multiplex panel. Which is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Exclude PML because every multiplex panel includes JCV.
Use current HIV OI guidance and host context to consider pathogens such as JCV/PML not necessarily included on routine panels, then select appropriate targeted evaluation.
Assume MS.
Stop evaluation because symptoms are chronic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A routine multiplex assay is not a universal pathogen screen; JCV/PML and other opportunistic CNS disease require context-specific consideration and tests. NIH HIV OI chapters are living guidance.
