topicGaps: There is no public full BIDMC didactic curriculum verified; institutional rotations/case volume are therefore not represented.
Cognitive, movement, MS, sleep and neuro-oncology are separate listed institutional tracks, but the selected recordings are a broad sampler and do not establish track-specific competency.
No adult/pediatric BIDMC child-neurology residency is listed in this packet; Pediatric EEG/Epilepsy is explicitly part of the posted line, but the full pediatric training syllabus was not verified.

Observed unique free recording coverage is 28.202 hours across 28 recordings, including 25.937 specialty hours, 0.462 foundation hours, and 1.803 supplementary pediatric hours; the 36-hour video floor remains short by 7.798 hours. Original scripts/plans are not rendered media and do not count.

The new AAN recordings broaden vestibular, headache, pregnancy-related cerebrovascular, neurogenetic, peripheral nerve, neuro-ophthalmic, carotid, ALS palliative, Parkinson and sleep lecture exposure; this is not a complete fellowship curriculum or competency assessment.

No dedicated full lectures with verified runtime were added for several domains, including deep EEG interpretation/status care, neurocritical prognostication, detailed pediatric EEG/epilepsy, current MS/MOGAD mimic criteria, sleep-study interpretation, dementia biomarkers, or track-specific clinical procedures. Use current criteria/guidelines and supervised training; original episode scripts address selected reasoning gaps only.
BIDMC does not publish a complete common didactic schedule in the cited directory; these recordings do not establish its rotations, volumes, accreditation, eligibility or actual curriculum.

The clinical content is a broad neurology fellow-level study set and is not a simulation of every track’s formal curriculum.
sourceCaveats: The input title “Neurology Fellowship” is the institutional page heading/category, not a unique board-defined specialty or one single clinical curriculum. BIDMC page lists separate programmes; research options are not physician clinical training.

BIDMC public category page does not itself state each track’s ACGME accreditation, admissions/eligibility, duration or full curriculum. One programme detail link was identified but not independently fully verified; contact programme for current details.

ABPN online certification pages change. Board eligibility must be individually confirmed; course completion confers none. Sleep exam is administered by ABIM under a co-sponsored assessment according to ABPN directory, not an ABPN-administered exam.

Clinical board and guideline qualifiers checked on 2026-10-07. Public teaching recordings are not comprehensive blueprints; some predate current criteria/guidelines. Audit current sources before real clinical use.

Public YouTube runtime/player data verified for counted canonical video IDs; videos remain copyrighted by their respective creators. Free watching does not grant downloading, editing, embedding rights or permission to copy slides/images.
Yale Panopto and most unverified UW archives were excluded because durations and/or public access could not be observed. No authentication workaround or stateful browser was used.
Authentic cases remain source-hosted and may contain controlled clinical images; do not copy/rehost. Constructed practice prompts are explicitly fictional.
No patient records or clinical image files have been copied; no diagnosis, volume benchmark, therapy direction or patient-specific advice is supplied.

Human clinical review is NOT PERFORMED. Independent educational study confers no affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, certification or guaranteed examination outcome.

topicGaps: There is no public full BIDMC didactic curriculum verified; institutional rotations/case volume are therefore not represented.
Cognitive, movement, MS, sleep and neuro-oncology are separate listed institutional tracks, but the selected recordings are a broad sampler and do not establish track-specific competency.
No adult/pediatric BIDMC child-neurology residency is listed in this packet; Pediatric EEG/Epilepsy is explicitly part of the posted line, but the full pediatric training syllabus was not verified.

Observed unique free recording coverage is 28.202 hours across 28 recordings, including 25.937 specialty hours, 0.462 foundation hours, and 1.803 supplementary pediatric hours; the 36-hour video floor remains short by 7.798 hours. Original scripts/plans are not rendered media and do not count.

The new AAN recordings broaden vestibular, headache, pregnancy-related cerebrovascular, neurogenetic, peripheral nerve, neuro-ophthalmic, carotid, ALS palliative, Parkinson and sleep lecture exposure; this is not a complete fellowship curriculum or competency assessment.

No dedicated full lectures with verified runtime were added for several domains, including deep EEG interpretation/status care, neurocritical prognostication, detailed pediatric EEG/epilepsy, current MS/MOGAD mimic criteria, sleep-study interpretation, dementia biomarkers, or track-specific clinical procedures. Use current criteria/guidelines and supervised training; original episode scripts address selected reasoning gaps only.
BIDMC does not publish a complete common didactic schedule in the cited directory; these recordings do not establish its rotations, volumes, accreditation, eligibility or actual curriculum.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult develops abrupt expressive language difficulty and right arm weakness. Which localization best fits the combined findings?

options.text: Right cerebellar hemisphere
Left dominant cerebral hemisphere network
Peripheral radial nerve
Neuromuscular junction

practiceQuestions.rationale: A dominant left hemispheric network can account for aphasia and contralateral motor weakness. Confirm details on examination and imaging; the vignette is not a real patient.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has symmetric distal sensory symptoms in the feet with reduced distal sensory amplitudes and relatively preserved conduction velocity on a teaching nerve-conduction trace. Which broad physiologic pattern is most consistent?

options.text: Axonal loss pattern
Pure neuromuscular-junction transmission failure
Central demyelinating lesion
Primary cerebellar syndrome

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reduced amplitudes with comparatively preserved velocities support an axonal pattern in context; electrodiagnostic interpretation requires full study and clinical correlation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A transient event is described as a brief unilateral sensory march followed by impaired awareness and post-event confusion. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Label epilepsy from the description alone
Characterize onset, evolution, recovery and competing mimics, then select appropriate evaluation
Assume syncope because awareness changed
Use a normal interictal EEG to exclude seizure

practiceQuestions.rationale: Semiology and context guide a differential; no single described feature or normal interictal EEG alone establishes/excludes epilepsy. Apply current ILAE classification after deciding whether an epileptic seizure occurred.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient develops new focal deficits. Which datum is especially important to document early when considering acute stroke pathways?

options.text: Last known well / onset chronology
Favorite hand
Remote family history of tremor
Whether symptoms improve with caffeine

practiceQuestions.rationale: Time course and last-known-well influence time-sensitive stroke evaluation. Actual imaging, eligibility and therapy decisions require current local protocols and qualified clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: An older adult has months of cognitive decline and visual hallucinations with fluctuations and parkinsonism. What is the most defensible conclusion from this vignette?

options.text: Lewy body dementia is a reasonable syndrome-level consideration, not pathologic proof
Alzheimer pathology is proven
A single biomarker is mandatory for every diagnosis
Delirium is excluded by chronic symptoms

practiceQuestions.rationale: This cluster supports consideration of a Lewy-body-spectrum syndrome, but clinical phenotype does not prove pathology and mixed causes are possible. Evaluate timeline, function, medications and alternatives.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with a possible first demyelinating event has a few nonspecific white-matter lesions. Which approach is sound?

options.text: Diagnose MS from lesion count alone
Integrate syndrome, dissemination evidence, exclusion of mimics and current criteria
Treat every nonspecific lesion as MS
Ignore spinal cord and clinical evidence

practiceQuestions.rationale: MS diagnosis requires an appropriate clinical context and criteria-based evidence; incidental/nonspecific lesions alone are insufficient. Check current diagnostic criteria version and specialist sources.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has burning feet and normal routine nerve conduction studies. Which statement is most appropriate?

options.text: Small-fiber neuropathy is impossible
Normal routine large-fiber studies may coexist with small-fiber dysfunction; pursue context-appropriate evaluation
This proves a functional disorder
Skin biopsy alone determines etiology

practiceQuestions.rationale: Routine nerve conduction studies primarily assess large fibers and may be normal in isolated small-fiber disorders. Further tests and cause evaluation depend on context and local standards.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient with a brain mass has a new seizure and worsening alertness. What is the safest educational response?

options.text: Treat as a nonurgent outpatient issue without reassessment
Flag possible neurologic emergency and require prompt clinician evaluation under local protocol
Assume tumor progression from one symptom
Give a specific antiseizure dose from this course

practiceQuestions.rationale: New seizure with deteriorating consciousness can signal an urgent neurologic problem; real care must be performed by qualified clinicians using local emergency pathways.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient reports nocturnal vocalization and dream enactment, plus daytime sleepiness. What is the best next step in reasoning?

options.text: Assume a single neurodegenerative diagnosis
Take structured sleep/medication history and consider sleep testing/referral while assessing safety
Diagnose epilepsy from nocturnal movements alone
Dismiss as normal aging

practiceQuestions.rationale: History, medications, timing and differential matter; sleep testing may be appropriate. The symptoms alone are not diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: An older public lecture describes a treatment algorithm from several years ago. How should a learner use it?

options.text: Apply verbatim to current patients
Treat it as historical teaching, check contemporary official guidance and local protocols before clinical application
Assume AAN video hosting means every claim is current
Use course quiz performance as prescribing authority

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public educational content can become outdated. Cross-check date-sensitive clinical recommendations with current authoritative guidance; this course does not authorize care.
